The Shannon index, borrowed from information theory and written H prime, is the negative sum over species of p times the natural logarithm of p, where p is the proportion of all individuals belonging to that species. It is sensitive to rare species and typically ranges from about 1.5 to 3.5 in real communities. The Simpson index, D, is the sum of p squared, giving the probability that two individuals drawn at random are the same species; it is usually reported as 1 minus D or as 1 over D, and it weights common species heavily. Because these indices confound richness and evenness in different ways, modern practice increasingly favours Hill numbers, which express diversity as an effective number of species at a chosen sensitivity q, where q equals 0 gives richness, q equals 1 the exponential of Shannon and q equals 2 the inverse Simpson. Their advantage is that the units are interpretable: a Hill number of 12 means the community is as diverse as twelve equally abundant species would be.

Two further ideas complete the descriptive toolkit. Robert Whittaker in 1960 distinguished alpha diversity, the diversity within one site, beta diversity, the turnover in species composition between sites, and gamma diversity, the total across a whole region. This matters enormously in conservation, because a region can have modest alpha diversity everywhere yet very high gamma diversity if each site holds a different set, meaning that protecting one representative site protects very little. The second idea is the species-abundance distribution, the pattern of how many species are common and how many rare. Almost every community ever surveyed shows the same shape: a few very abundant species, more moderately common ones and a long tail of rarities, often approximating a lognormal distribution. This universality is a genuine puzzle, since several quite different theoretical models predict it, which means the shape alone cannot tell you which process generated it. Finally, all these measures depend on sampling effort, because rare species accumulate as you look harder, so honest comparison requires either equal effort or a rarefaction procedure that standardises it.

sections.heading: The Niche: What a Species Does and Where It Can Live
sections.body:
The niche concept is the central organising idea of community ecology, and it has meant three different things at different times, which causes endless confusion. Joseph Grinnell in 1917 used it to mean the set of environmental conditions and habitat a species requires: essentially an address. Charles Elton in 1927 used it to mean the species' functional role in the community, what it eats and what eats it: essentially a profession. G. Evelyn Hutchinson unified these in 1957 with a formulation that has proved extraordinarily durable. He defined the niche as an n-dimensional hypervolume, where each dimension is an environmental variable or resource axis, such as temperature, humidity, soil pH, prey size or shade tolerance, and the volume is the region of that space within which the species can maintain a viable population.

Hutchinson's crucial distinction was between the fundamental niche, the full hypervolume a species could occupy in the absence of interference from other species, and the realised niche, the smaller portion it actually occupies once competitors, predators and parasites are present. The realised niche is almost always a subset of the fundamental one, and the difference is a direct measure of biotic pressure. Joseph Connell's 1961 experiments on Scottish rocky shores gave the classic demonstration. Two barnacles occupy distinct bands: Chthamalus high on the shore, Semibalanus lower down. Removing Semibalanus allowed Chthamalus to spread downwards and thrive, showing its fundamental niche extended far below its realised one and that competition, in the form of Semibalanus physically undercutting and crushing it, set the lower limit. Removing Chthamalus did not allow Semibalanus upwards, because its upper limit was set by physical desiccation, not competition. One boundary was biotic, the other abiotic, and only an experiment could tell them apart.

That asymmetry turns out to be a broad pattern. Across many systems, the harsh end of an environmental gradient is governed by physiological tolerance and the benign end by competition, which is one of the sturdier generalisations the field has produced. Two refinements are worth carrying. First, niches are not fixed properties: they can shift over ecological time through behavioural flexibility and over evolutionary time through selection, so a species introduced to a new continent may occupy a different realised niche than at home, which is why niche models based on a species' native range routinely underpredict where an invader can establish. Second, the concept has an important limitation that took decades to appreciate. If each species requires a distinct niche, and niche axes are finite, then diversity should be limited in a way that flatly contradicts the observed coexistence of hundreds of apparently similar tree species in a tropical forest or dozens of planktonic algae in a well-mixed lake. Hutchinson himself named the latter the paradox of the plankton in 1961, and resolving it drove much of the theory that followed.

sections.heading: Competition, Exclusion and How Species Divide Resources
sections.body:
Competition occurs when two individuals both require something in short supply, so that use by one reduces availability to the other. It comes in two forms. Exploitation competition is indirect: each simply consumes the shared resource, and neither need ever encounter the other, as when two plant species draw down the same soil nitrogen. Interference competition is direct: one individual actively prevents another's access, through aggression, territoriality, overgrowth or chemical means, as when a barnacle undercuts its neighbour or a walnut tree releases juglone that suppresses nearby seedlings. Competition can be intraspecific, within a species, or interspecific, between species, and intraspecific competition is almost always the more intense of the two because members of the same species need exactly the same things.

The theoretical backbone is the Lotka-Volterra competition model, developed independently by Alfred Lotka in 1925 and Vito Volterra in 1926. It extends the logistic growth equation by adding, for each species, a term reducing its effective population by the abundance of the other multiplied by a competition coefficient alpha, which expresses how strongly one individual of the competitor suppresses growth relative to one individual of the species itself. Analysing the model gives a clean and important result: stable coexistence requires that each species inhibits itself more than it inhibits the other. If interspecific competition exceeds intraspecific competition for either species, one wins and the other is driven out. Georgii Gause demonstrated this experimentally in 1934 with Paramecium in laboratory culture, where two species grown together on the same bacterial food reliably ended with one extinct, and the generalisation became known as the competitive exclusion principle: complete competitors cannot coexist.

The obvious objection is that nature is full of apparently similar species living together, and the classical resolution is resource partitioning. Robert MacArthur's 1958 study of five warbler species in the same New England spruce trees showed that each concentrated its feeding in a different zone of the canopy and used somewhat different foraging manoeuvres, so their realised niches were separated even though their habitat was shared. Where partitioning has an evolutionary component it produces character displacement, in which two species differ more where they coexist than where each occurs alone. The best-documented case is the Galápagos ground finches studied by Peter and Rosemary Grant, where beak depths diverge on islands shared by two species; a 2006 paper documented a measurable shift in Geospiza fortis beak size within a single year after a competitor arrived. Two honest caveats belong here. First, competition is hard to demonstrate from pattern alone, because species can differ for reasons having nothing to do with each other, a criticism pressed forcefully by Daniel Simberloff and colleagues in the 1980s null-model debates. Second, competition is often intermittent, intense only in bad years, and therefore easy to miss in short studies.

sections.heading: Predation, Herbivory and the Dynamics They Generate
sections.body:
Consumption of one organism by another is the interaction that most visibly structures communities, and it spans a spectrum. True predators kill and consume multiple prey. Grazers and browsers consume parts of many plants without usually killing them. Parasites live on or in a single host, reducing its fitness without typically killing it, while parasitoids, chiefly certain wasps and flies, develop inside a host and reliably kill it, an arrangement so effective that parasitoids may constitute around ten per cent of all described insect species. Each has different population consequences, but all share the property that the consumer's success depends on prey abundance and the prey's mortality depends on consumer abundance, which is the recipe for coupled dynamics.

The Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model captures the essence in two equations: prey grow exponentially in the absence of predators and are removed in proportion to the product of the two abundances, while predators die off exponentially without prey and are produced in proportion to that same product. The model predicts sustained oscillations in which predator peaks lag prey peaks by roughly a quarter of a cycle, which is exactly what is seen in the famous Hudson's Bay Company fur records for Canada lynx and snowshoe hare, cycling with a period of about ten years across more than a century. The model is nonetheless too simple in important ways: its cycles are neutrally stable, meaning any disturbance permanently changes the amplitude, which is not how real systems behave, and the lynx-hare cycle is now understood to be driven substantially by hare food supply and by predator diversity rather than lynx alone. Adding prey self-limitation and a saturating predator response makes the model more realistic.

That saturating response is the functional response, classified by C. S. Holling in 1959 into three types. Type I is a straight line, consumption rising in proportion to prey density; Type II rises and then plateaus, because a predator needs handling time to subdue and eat each item, so there is a ceiling on intake no matter how abundant prey become; Type III is S-shaped, with low consumption at low prey density because the predator switches to alternative food or has not yet formed a search image. The distinction has real consequences: Type II predation is destabilising and can drive prey to extinction at low density, while Type III provides a low-density refuge and is stabilising. Predation also shapes communities without killing anything, through trait-mediated effects: prey that hide, feed less or move elsewhere pay a cost in growth and reproduction, and several studies suggest these non-consumptive effects can rival direct mortality in magnitude. Finally, predation drives some of the most elaborate evolution known, from cryptic and warning coloration to tetrodotoxin arms races between newts and garter snakes, in which local prey toxicity and predator resistance have escalated to levels far beyond what either needs elsewhere.

sections.heading: Keystone Species and Trophic Cascades
sections.body:
In 1966 Robert Paine removed the predatory starfish Pisaster ochraceus from a stretch of rocky intertidal shore at Mukkaw Bay, Washington, and kept removing it. Within a few years the number of species in the plot fell from fifteen to eight. The mussel Mytilus californianus, previously kept in check by starfish predation, monopolised the rock and crowded out barnacles, algae and everything else. Paine coined the term keystone species for an organism whose effect on community structure is disproportionately large relative to its abundance, taking the metaphor from the wedge-shaped stone at the top of an arch whose removal collapses the whole structure. The experiment is a landmark partly for its result and partly for its method: it demonstrated that community structure could be tested by manipulation rather than only described.

The related idea is the trophic cascade, in which the effect of a predator propagates down through successive trophic levels, alternating in sign. The classic marine case is the sea otter. Where otters are present they eat sea urchins; urchin numbers stay low; kelp survives and forms dense forests supporting many species. Where otters were hunted out, urchins proliferated and grazed kelp forests down to bare rock, the so-called urchin barrens, a transformation documented across the North Pacific by James Estes and colleagues from the 1970s onward. The pattern is three trophic levels with predators benefiting plants, and it has been shown in lakes, streams, grasslands and forests. Cascades are generally strongest in aquatic systems with relatively simple food chains and weaker in complex terrestrial ones where consumers have many alternative prey and plants have many defences.

The most famous cascade is also the one where honesty is most needed. After wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in 1995, a widely repeated account held that wolves reduced elk numbers and changed elk behaviour, which allowed willow and aspen to regrow, which stabilised riverbanks and even changed the course of rivers. Elements of this are well supported: wolves did reduce elk numbers substantially, and willow recovery has occurred in places. But the strong version has been seriously challenged. Later work has argued that the behavioural landscape-of-fear effect is much weaker than claimed, that willow recovery is patchy and depends heavily on water tables and beaver activity, that concurrent drought, bear and cougar predation and human hunting all contributed to elk decline, and that the river-course claim is not supportable. The honest summary is that Yellowstone shows a real but complicated and contested cascade whose popular telling outran its evidence. Two further cautions apply to the keystone idea generally: which species is a keystone depends on context and can change with conditions, and the label has been stretched to the point where it is sometimes used simply to mean important, which drains it of meaning.

sections.heading: Mutualism, Facilitation and the Positive Interactions
sections.body:
For most of the twentieth century community ecology was preoccupied with the negative interactions, competition and predation, and treated cooperation as a curiosity. That balance has shifted decisively. Interactions are classified by their sign for each partner: competition is minus minus, predation and parasitism minus plus, commensalism plus zero, amensalism minus zero, and mutualism plus plus. Mutualisms turn out to be pervasive and often foundational. Roughly eighty per cent of land plant species form mycorrhizal associations, in which fungi extend the effective root system enormously in exchange for photosynthetic carbon, and this partnership is thought to have been essential to the colonisation of land in the Ordovician, around 450 million years ago. Around eighty-seven per cent of flowering plants depend to some degree on animal pollination. Corals are animals only in part; their productivity comes from symbiotic dinoflagellate algae, and bleaching is the loss of that partnership.

Mutualisms are best understood not as altruism but as reciprocal exploitation that happens to pay both parties, and this framing predicts their weaknesses correctly. Because each partner would do better still if it could take the benefit without paying, mutualisms are perpetually vulnerable to cheating, and stable ones generally have some mechanism controlling it: partner choice, sanctions such as legumes reducing oxygen supply to nodules of rhizobia that fix little nitrogen, physical structures restricting access, or simple spatial constraint that ties partners together. Mutualisms also range from obligate, where neither survives alone, as with yucca and yucca moth or fig and fig wasp, to facultative and diffuse, where dozens of species interchangeably fill the role, as with most temperate pollination. Obligate specialised mutualisms are spectacular and fragile; diffuse ones are unremarkable and robust, which matters greatly for conservation risk assessment.

Facilitation is the broader idea that one species makes conditions better for another without any exchange. A cushion plant on an alpine screen slope moderates wind and temperature under its canopy, and dozens of other species establish there and nowhere else. Nurse plants in deserts shade seedlings that would otherwise cook. Mussel beds and oyster reefs create habitat structure for hundreds of associated species; such organisms are called ecosystem engineers, a term introduced by Clive Jones and colleagues in 1994, with beavers as the standard example. The stress gradient hypothesis, proposed by Ragan Callaway and Lauren Walker in 1997, makes the general prediction that facilitation dominates under harsh physical conditions while competition dominates under benign ones, and it has reasonable but not universal support. The practical significance is considerable: restoration that ignores facilitation often fails, because planting widely spaced individuals in a stressful site removes exactly the mutual sheltering that lets the species establish, and clumped planting frequently outperforms even though it looks like it should intensify competition.

sections.heading: Food Webs, Trophic Levels and the Flow of Energy
sections.body:
A food web is a map of who eats whom, and it is the most complete single description of a community's structure. The simplified version is the food chain, an ordered sequence of trophic levels: primary producers, which fix energy from sunlight or chemical sources; primary consumers, the herbivores; secondary consumers, which eat herbivores; tertiary consumers; and, running alongside all of them, the decomposers and detritivores that process dead material. Real webs are far messier than chains. Most consumers feed at more than one level, an arrangement called omnivory, and most prey are eaten by many predators, so a real web is a dense tangle in which trophic level is better treated as a continuous average than an integer. Stable isotope analysis, using the enrichment of nitrogen-15 by roughly 3.4 parts per thousand per trophic step, is now the standard way of measuring an organism's actual average position.

The energetics impose hard limits on structure. Only around one to two per cent of incident solar energy is captured by photosynthesis, and thereafter roughly ten per cent of the energy at one trophic level is incorporated into the next, the rest being lost to respiration, to unconsumed or indigestible material and to heat, as required by the second law of thermodynamics. The ten per cent figure is a rough average with real variation, from perhaps two per cent in some terrestrial systems to over thirty per cent in some aquatic ones, but the direction is inescapable. Because of it, food chains are short, rarely exceeding four or five levels, top predators are necessarily rare, and a pyramid of biomass usually narrows upward. There is a well-known exception: in open ocean plankton systems the phytoplankton have a very rapid turnover, so standing biomass of producers can be lower than that of the consumers they support, producing an inverted biomass pyramid even though the pyramid of energy flow is never inverted.

Food web ecologists measure several structural properties. Connectance is the fraction of all possible links that actually exist, typically only about ten per cent in well-resolved webs. Chain length, degree of omnivory, and the frequency of particular three-species motifs all have consequences for dynamics. Two results deserve emphasis. First, interaction strengths within webs are highly skewed: a few strong links and very many weak ones, and theory suggests that the abundance of weak links is itself stabilising, because weak interactions damp the oscillations that strong ones generate. Second, the practical difficulty of constructing food webs is severe and shapes what we think we know. Diets are hard to observe, rare links are missed, taxonomic resolution is uneven, with parasites in particular historically omitted despite being extremely numerous, and published webs from the same system by different workers can differ substantially. Molecular gut-content and faecal metabarcoding have improved this markedly since around 2010, and they routinely reveal links that observation missed entirely.

sections.heading: Succession: How Communities Change Over Time
sections.body:
Communities are not static. Succession is the directional change in composition following a disturbance or the appearance of new ground. Primary succession begins on substrate that has never supported a community: fresh lava, a glacial moraine, a new sand dune, bare rock. It is slow, because soil must be built, and it typically starts with organisms tolerant of extreme conditions and able to obtain nutrients from air or rock, lichens and nitrogen-fixing plants prominent among them. Secondary succession begins where a community has been removed but soil, seed bank and often surviving roots remain, as after fire, windthrow, flood or abandonment of farmland, and it is much faster. An abandoned field in temperate eastern North America typically passes through annual weeds within one to three years, perennial herbs and grasses over five to fifteen, shrubs and fast-growing pines or birches over roughly fifteen to fifty, and shade-tolerant hardwoods over a century or more.

The interpretation of this pattern produced one of ecology's defining arguments. Frederic Clements, writing from 1916, saw succession as a highly deterministic process in which a community developed like a superorganism through predictable stages toward a single stable climax determined by regional climate. Henry Gleason, from 1926, argued the opposite individualistic view: species respond independently to environment and to chance dispersal, communities are simply whatever assemblage happens to result, and the apparent unity is in the observer's eye. The weight of evidence, particularly from studies of pollen cores showing that tree species moved individually and at different rates after the last glaciation rather than migrating as intact communities, favours Gleason substantially, though modern thinking recognises that strong interactions do create some genuine community-level coherence.

Mechanistically, Joseph Connell and Ralph Slatyer proposed in 1977 three models that remain the standard framework, and all three occur in real systems. In the facilitation model, early colonists modify conditions in ways that make the site suitable for later species and unsuitable for themselves, which is the classic primary-succession story of lichens producing soil and nitrogen fixers such as Dryas enriching it. In the tolerance model, later species simply tolerate lower resource levels and win by persistence regardless of what came before. In the inhibition model, whoever arrives first holds the site and later species enter only when the incumbent dies, making outcome heavily dependent on arrival order, a phenomenon called priority effect. Two further points matter practically. Succession does not always converge on one endpoint; the same starting site can settle into different stable states depending on early arrivals and disturbance history, which is why restoration outcomes are hard to guarantee. And the classical notion of a permanent climax has largely been abandoned, because disturbance is frequent enough in most landscapes that mature communities are better described as a shifting mosaic of patches of different ages.

sections.heading: Why Diversity Varies: Latitude, Area and Islands
sections.body:
The most conspicuous pattern in the distribution of life is the latitudinal diversity gradient: species richness rises steeply from the poles toward the equator in almost every group examined, on land and at sea, for the present day and through much of the fossil record. The magnitude is startling. A hectare of Amazonian or Bornean forest may hold 300 or more tree species; a hectare of temperate deciduous forest holds perhaps 10 to 30; a boreal forest 1 to 5. The gradient has attracted well over thirty proposed explanations and no consensus, which is worth stating plainly rather than picking a favourite. The leading candidates are greater solar energy and productivity supporting more individuals and therefore more viable populations; longer evolutionary time in tropical regions that were less disturbed by Pleistocene glaciation; faster diversification rates in warm environments; more stable climates permitting narrower niches; and stronger biotic interactions, particularly specialised natural enemies, preventing any one species from dominating. These are not mutually exclusive and the honest position is that several probably operate together.

The second robust pattern is far better understood. The species-area relationship states that larger areas hold more species according to S equals c times A raised to the power z, where A is area and z is an exponent usually falling between 0.15 and 0.35 for samples within a continuous habitat, and higher, around 0.25 to 0.4, for genuine islands. Because z is well below one, the relationship has a specific and important consequence: a tenfold reduction in habitat area with z equal to 0.25 predicts loss of roughly forty-four per cent of species, since 10 raised to the power minus 0.25 is about 0.56. This is the basis of most extinction projections from habitat loss, and although the exact translation is debated, the qualitative conclusion that halving a habitat costs far more than nothing but far less than half its species is solid.

Robert MacArthur and Edward O. Wilson combined these ideas in 1967 into the theory of island biogeography, one of the most influential models in ecology. It proposes that the number of species on an island reaches a dynamic equilibrium where the immigration rate of new species equals the extinction rate of resident ones. Immigration falls as more species accumulate, since fewer remain in the pool, and falls with distance from the mainland; extinction rises with more species, since each is less abundant, and falls with island area. The theory therefore predicts that large near islands hold the most species and small remote ones the fewest, and crucially that composition keeps turning over even when the total stays constant. Daniel Simberloff and Wilson tested it directly in the 1960s by fumigating tiny mangrove islets in the Florida Keys and watching recolonisation, and species numbers did return to close to their original levels while the identities differed. The theory was rapidly adopted as a framework for reserve design, though applying it uncritically to habitat fragments has been criticised, since fragments are embedded in a matrix that is hostile rather than lethal and permits movement that true ocean does not.

sections.heading: Disturbance, Patch Dynamics and Intermediate Disturbance
sections.body:
Disturbance is any relatively discrete event that removes biomass and frees resources: fire, storm, flood, landslide, treefall, ice scour, drought, disease outbreak, grazing or human clearance. For most of the twentieth century disturbance was treated as an interruption of the proper order of things. It is now understood as an intrinsic and often necessary component of how communities work. Many species require it outright. Jack pine and several other conifers have serotinous cones sealed with resin that open only in fire's heat. Fire-suppressed grasslands convert to shrubland and lose most of their herbaceous diversity within a few decades. Floodplain forests depend on periodic scouring to create the bare wet sediment their seedlings need, which is why dam construction so reliably eliminates cottonwood and willow regeneration downstream.

Disturbance regimes are described by frequency, intensity, size, and season, and it is the whole regime rather than any single event that determines what a community looks like. A system adapted to frequent low-intensity ground fire, such as longleaf pine savanna burning every two to five years, is transformed by several decades of suppression into one carrying enough fuel for a catastrophic crown fire that its own species cannot survive. This dynamic is the central reason fire management in much of North America and Australia has moved toward reinstating regular controlled burning rather than excluding fire, and it illustrates the general principle that changing a disturbance regime can be more damaging than the disturbance itself. The same logic applies to rivers, where the natural flow regime including its floods is now treated as the thing to be restored rather than an inconvenience to be regulated away.

The best-known theoretical statement is the intermediate disturbance hypothesis, associated principally with Joseph Connell's 1978 paper on coral reefs and rainforests. It proposes that diversity peaks at intermediate frequency and intensity of disturbance: too little and competitively dominant species monopolise the site, too much and only fast-colonising disturbance-tolerant species persist, while in between both persist because dominants are periodically knocked back before they can exclude anyone. The idea is intuitive, widely taught, and has been sharply criticised. A 2013 analysis by Kevin Fox found that the hump-shaped pattern appears in only a minority of empirical tests and that the underlying theoretical justification is weaker than assumed, since disturbance alone does not create the negative frequency dependence that coexistence actually requires. A fair summary is that intermediate disturbance is a useful heuristic which sometimes describes reality but is not a general law, and that the more defensible general statement is the patch dynamics view: disturbance creates a shifting mosaic of patches at different successional stages, and a landscape containing all stages simultaneously supports more species than one uniformly at any single stage. That formulation is what most practical conservation management now works from.

sections.heading: Neutral Theory and Modern Coexistence Theory
sections.body:
In 2001 Stephen Hubbell published a book proposing something deliberately provocative: that many large-scale community patterns can be reproduced by a model in which all individuals of all species are assumed ecologically identical, with equal birth, death and dispersal rates, and community composition drifts by pure chance, replenished by random speciation. This neutral theory of biodiversity has only a few parameters, and it predicts observed species-abundance distributions and species-area relationships in tropical forests remarkably well. Nobody, including Hubbell, believes species really are identical. The point was that matching the pattern does not validate the assumptions, which is a serious warning to a field that had often inferred niche processes directly from patterns. If a model assuming no niches at all reproduces the data, then reproducing the data cannot be evidence for niches.

The response reframed the whole coexistence question, chiefly through Peter Chesson's synthesis published in 2000. Chesson's framework separates two distinct things a species needs. Equalising mechanisms reduce the average fitness difference between species, making them more similar in competitive ability, which slows exclusion but cannot prevent it. Stabilising mechanisms create negative frequency dependence, meaning each species does relatively better when it is rare, which actively pulls populations back from the brink and genuinely permits coexistence. The formal criterion is the invasion test: species coexist if each can increase from low abundance when the others are at equilibrium. The critical insight is that coexistence requires niche differences, meaning stabilisation, to exceed fitness differences; large niche differences permit coexistence even between unequal competitors, while near-identical species coexist only if their fitness is also nearly identical, which is essentially the neutral case.

Chesson's framework accommodates mechanisms that earlier theory struggled with. The storage effect allows species to coexist by responding differently to a fluctuating environment while having a long-lived stage, such as a seed bank or an adult tree, that stores the gains from good years through bad ones; it is a leading explanation for the coexistence of desert annuals and of plankton. Relative nonlinearity of competition allows coexistence when species differ in how their growth responds to resource fluctuations. Janzen-Connell effects, proposed independently by Daniel Janzen in 1970 and Joseph Connell in 1971, provide strong stabilisation through species-specific natural enemies concentrated near parent trees, so seedlings survive better far from conspecific adults; the mechanism is now well supported by experiments showing soil-pathogen-mediated negative density dependence, and it is a leading explanation for tropical tree diversity. The productive modern position is that neutral drift and niche processes both operate, their relative importance varies with scale and system, and the interesting empirical question is the mixture rather than which one is right.

sections.heading: Metacommunities: Communities Connected Across Space
sections.body:
Treating a community as a closed box is a convenient fiction. Real communities exchange individuals with their neighbours, and once dispersal is admitted the explanation of local composition changes fundamentally. The metacommunity concept, formalised by Mathew Leibold and colleagues in 2004, defines a metacommunity as a set of local communities linked by dispersal of multiple potentially interacting species, and identifies four idealised paradigms that make different predictions. Species sorting assumes dispersal is sufficient to reach suitable sites but not so heavy as to override local conditions, so each species ends up where its niche fits and composition tracks the environment; this is the closest to classical niche theory and is empirically the commonest outcome. Mass effects assume dispersal is so high that immigration sustains populations even in unsuitable patches, producing source-sink structure in which a species is found where it could not persist alone.

The other two paradigms complete the space. The patch dynamics view assumes patches are identical and species trade off colonisation ability against competitive ability, so a superior competitor and a superior disperser coexist regionally by occupying different patches at different times, a mechanism formalised long before as the competition-colonisation trade-off. The neutral view assumes species are equivalent and composition is set by dispersal limitation and drift. These are not rival theories so much as regions of a continuum defined by how much dispersal there is and how much environmental heterogeneity, and most real systems sit somewhere in between, which is why the modern practice is to partition observed variation in composition statistically between environmental and spatial components rather than to declare a system to be one type.

The practical importance is hard to overstate. Dispersal limitation means that a site may lack a species simply because nothing arrived, not because conditions are wrong, which explains why restoration projects frequently stall: the physical habitat is repaired but the species pool cannot reach it across an agricultural or urban matrix, and deliberate reintroduction is required. Source-sink structure means that a population apparently thriving in a monitored patch may be entirely dependent on immigration from an unmonitored source elsewhere, so protecting the visibly abundant site while losing the source destroys both. Habitat fragmentation acts principally by cutting dispersal, which is the reasoning behind wildlife corridors, stepping-stone reserves and the general principle that connected reserve networks outperform isolated ones of the same total area. And because rescue effects from neighbouring patches buffer local extinction, an intact metacommunity is far more resilient than the same patches would be in isolation, which is one of the strongest general arguments in landscape-scale conservation planning. It also explains why a reserve that has been isolated for a long time keeps losing species for decades afterwards even though nothing further is done to it, a phenomenon known as faunal relaxation.

sections.heading: Applied Community Ecology: Invasions, Restoration and Management
sections.body:
The clearest test of whether community ecology understands anything is whether it can predict what happens when communities are altered, and invasions are the largest unplanned experiment available. Only a small fraction of introduced species establish and a smaller fraction still become damaging, a rough and much debated rule of thumb sometimes stated as ten per cent at each stage. Several hypotheses explain why some succeed. Enemy release proposes that an introduced species leaves its specialised predators, parasites and pathogens behind and is therefore freed from a control that limits it at home, which is the rationale for classical biological control. The novel weapons hypothesis proposes that some invaders bring chemical or behavioural traits against which resident species have no evolved defence. Propagule pressure, the sheer number and frequency of individuals introduced, is consistently one of the strongest single predictors and is also the most tractable to manage, since it argues directly for biosecurity at the point of transport.

Charles Elton proposed in 1958 that more diverse communities should be harder to invade, because their niches are more fully occupied. Testing this produced the invasion paradox: at small scales, experiments generally confirm that more diverse plots resist invasion better, while at large scales the correlation is usually positive, with species-rich regions holding more exotic species. The resolution is that at large scales both native and exotic richness respond to the same underlying drivers of productivity and heterogeneity, which swamps the local resistance effect. This is a textbook example of how spatial scale can reverse an ecological relationship, and of why scale must always be specified.

Management application follows directly from the theory. Biological control works when a specialist enemy is introduced against a target, and its history contains both spectacular successes, such as the cactus moth Cactoblastis clearing 25 million hectares of prickly pear in Australia after 1926, and notorious disasters, such as the cane toad introduced to Queensland in 1935 which failed against its target beetle and became a major invader itself, and the small Indian mongoose introduced to islands worldwide which devastated native birds and reptiles. Modern protocols require extensive host-specificity testing precisely because generalist agents cannot be recalled. Restoration must reckon with alternative stable states and priority effects, which is why simply removing a stressor often does not return the original community and why the order of reintroduction matters. Trophic rewilding attempts to restore missing interactions rather than species lists. And the concept of novel ecosystems acknowledges, controversially, that some assemblages of native and introduced species now function in ways that cannot be reversed at acceptable cost, forcing a choice between managing what exists and pursuing a historical baseline that may no longer be attainable under a changed climate.

sections.heading: Studying a Community: Sampling and Survey in Practice
sections.body: Community ecology is unusually dependent on the quality of its field data, and most flawed conclusions trace back to sampling rather than to reasoning. The core problem is that you can never count everything, so every result is an inference from a sample whose design determines what inferences are legitimate. Three decisions dominate: what the sampling unit is, how units are placed, and how much effort goes into each. The procedure below describes a general vegetation and ground-fauna survey of the kind an ecologist, land manager or capable amateur can run, and the same logic adapts to birds by point count, aquatic invertebrates by kick sample or mammals by camera trap.
steps: State the question and the comparison before designing anything. Estimating total richness, comparing two management treatments, and detecting change over time each require a different design, and a survey built for one answers the others badly.

Define the sampling unit and its size. Quadrats of 1 square metre suit grassland herbs, 10 by 10 metres suit shrubs, and 20 by 20 or larger suit trees; too small a unit misses large-bodied species, too large a one averages away the pattern you are looking for.

Place units by a rule that removes your own bias. Use random coordinates within the area, or a systematic grid with a random start, or stratified random placement if the site contains distinct habitat types that should each be represented.

Decide replication in advance and be honest about pseudoreplication: several quadrats inside one treated field are subsamples of one experimental unit, not independent replicates of the treatment, and analysing them as if they were inflates confidence enormously.

Record abundance in a defined and repeatable way. Counts of individuals, percentage cover estimated against a reference chart, or biomass all work, but cover estimates drift between observers, so calibrate everyone against the same quadrats at the start.
Standardise effort and conditions. Record date, time, weather, observer and search duration, because detectability varies with all of them and an apparent decline is often a change in conditions.

Identify to the finest level you can defend and keep vouchers or photographs of anything uncertain. Lumping difficult groups into one morphospecies is acceptable if declared, but silently misidentifying them corrupts everything downstream.
Build a species accumulation curve as you go, plotting cumulative species against units sampled. If it is still climbing steeply you have not sampled enough to compare richness with anywhere else.

Account for imperfect detection. Repeat visits to the same units allow occupancy or mark-recapture style estimators to separate a genuine absence from a failure to detect, which matters most for exactly the rare species that drive conservation decisions.

Analyse with the design in mind: rarefy or use coverage-based standardisation before comparing richness, use ordination such as non-metric multidimensional scaling to visualise composition, and report variability rather than only means.

Archive the raw data with full metadata, including zero counts and units where nothing was found, since absences carry as much information as presences and are the first thing lost from a spreadsheet.

sections.heading: Limits, Failure Modes and What the Field Cannot Yet Do
sections.body:
A guide to community ecology that closed on confident generalisations would misrepresent it. The field's predictive power is genuinely limited, and knowing where the limits fall is part of using it competently. The first limit is scale dependence. Relationships routinely reverse between scales, as with the diversity and invasibility relationship being negative in small plots and positive across regions, and a result reported without its spatial and temporal grain cannot be interpreted. The second is contingency. Outcomes depend on the particular species present, on arrival order through priority effects, and on climatic conditions during the study, so replicating a well-known experiment in a different place or a different decade quite often gives a different answer without either result being wrong.

The third limit is the difficulty of demonstrating causation. Most community data are observational, and correlations among species abundances are produced just as readily by shared responses to unmeasured environment as by interaction. Manipulative experiments solve this in principle but are constrained in practice: they are usually small, short and conducted on the tractable organisms, so the evidence base is skewed toward plots of a few square metres over a few growing seasons, and extrapolating from that to a forest over a century is an act of faith rather than inference. Long-term datasets such as the Rothamsted Park Grass experiment, running since 1856, or the Hubbard Brook watershed studies since 1963, are disproportionately valuable precisely because they are so rare, and repeatedly they have shown that conclusions drawn from three-year studies reversed once the record ran to thirty.

Several specific failure modes recur and are worth guarding against. Inferring competition from a negative correlation between two species' abundances, when both may simply prefer different soils. Treating a diversity index as if it were a measurement of ecosystem health, when a polluted site can score well by hosting many tolerant species. Assuming a keystone or cascade result from one system transfers to another, when it demonstrably often does not. Reading a stable community as evidence of equilibrium, when it may be slowly changing on a timescale longer than the observation. Applying a species-area extinction projection as if habitat loss were instantaneous and complete, when extinction debt means losses accumulate over decades and management can intervene. And the general failure of assuming reversibility: many community changes, including invasion, soil biota alteration and shifts to alternative stable states, do not simply undo when the cause is removed. The appropriate posture is neither dismissal nor overclaiming. Community ecology provides a strong set of mechanisms, a decent understanding of which ones matter where, and reliable qualitative guidance, while quantitative prediction of a particular community's future remains genuinely beyond its reach in most cases.

guides.title: Ecosystem Ecology and Energy Flow
guides.summary: How energy captured from sunlight and chemistry moves through living systems: primary production, trophic structure, ecological efficiency, decomposition, nutrient cycles, the productivity of Earth's biomes, the forces that regulate ecosystems, and what happens when they are disturbed or collapse.

sections.heading: What Ecosystem Ecology Studies
sections.body: Ecology is studied at nested scales: individual organisms, populations of one species, communities of interacting species, and finally ecosystems, where the living community is joined to its physical environment and the two are treated as a single working system. Ecosystem ecology asks the accountant's questions: how much energy enters this system, along what paths does it travel, where is it stored, and what leaves? How do carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and water move between soil, air, water, and living tissue? The word ecosystem was coined in 1935 by the British botanist Arthur Tansley, who insisted that organisms cannot be understood separately from the flows of matter and energy that sustain them, and the approach was made quantitative in 1942 by a young American limnologist, Raymond Lindeman, whose study of Cedar Bog Lake in Minnesota traced calories from sunlight through algae, zooplankton, and fish and founded what he called trophic dynamics, the analysis of feeding as energy transfer. His paper, published just after his death at age twenty-seven, remains one of the most influential in ecology. The perspective is powerful because it makes wildly different systems comparable: a coral reef, a wheat field, a sewage lagoon, and a beech forest can all be described by the same currencies, energy fixed per square meter per year and nutrients cycled per square meter per year, and the numbers reveal structure that lists of species never could. Two grand generalizations organize the whole subject, and they are worth stating at the outset because everything else elaborates them. First, energy flows but does not cycle. Energy enters ecosystems almost entirely as sunlight, is captured by photosynthesis, passes from eater to eaten a few steps at most, and at every step most of it is dissipated as low-grade heat that radiates away into space, never to be used again. An ecosystem must therefore be continuously powered; switch off the sun and the machine stops within months. Second, matter cycles but does not flow away. The atoms of carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus in living tissue are not consumed; they are borrowed, passed through food chains, released by decomposition, and reused, some of them circulating through organisms for billions of years. The nitrogen in your proteins has been thunderstruck, fixed by bacteria, dissolved in ancient seas, and exhaled by volcanoes. These two rules, one-way energy and round-trip matter, explain the deep architecture of life on Earth: why food chains are short, why big fierce animals are rare, why soils matter more than they appear to, why removing a predator can turn a kelp forest into barren rock, and why human appropriation of the biosphere's energy flow is among the most consequential facts of the modern age. This guide follows the energy from its capture to its dissipation, then follows the atoms around their loops, and ends with how the whole system responds to stress and what its failure looks like.

sections.heading: The Thermodynamics of Life
sections.body: Ecosystems are physical systems, and their behavior is disciplined by the two laws of thermodynamics as strictly as any steam engine. The first law says energy is conserved: it can be transformed, light into chemical bonds, chemical bonds into motion and heat, but never created or destroyed. Bookkeeping therefore works: every joule entering an ecosystem can in principle be tracked until it leaves, and ecologists build energy budgets exactly as engineers do. The second law says that every energy transformation is inefficient in a particular directional way: some of the energy is inevitably degraded into disordered thermal motion, heat at ambient temperature, which can do no further biological work. Living things are sometimes said to defy the second law by building improbable order from disorder, but they do no such thing; they are open systems, maintaining their internal order by continuously importing high-quality energy and exporting entropy as heat, exactly as a refrigerator stays cold by pumping heat out its back. The Austrian physicist Erwin Schrodinger popularized this view in his 1944 book What Is Life, describing organisms as feeding on negative entropy, and it is the correct frame for everything in ecology: an organism, a food chain, a forest are all dissipative structures, patterns maintained by a through-flow of energy, like a candle flame or a whirlpool, and like them they collapse when the flow stops. The numbers begin with the sun. Solar radiation arrives at the top of the atmosphere at an average of about 1,361 watts per square meter facing the sun, which spread over the whole rotating sphere averages around 340 watts per square meter; roughly thirty percent is reflected, and what reaches the ground averages a couple of hundred watts per square meter, varying enormously with latitude, season, and cloud. Of the light that actually strikes vegetation, only the band between roughly 400 and 700 nanometers, about forty-five percent of the total energy, is usable by photosynthesis, and the photosynthetic machinery itself has a theoretical maximum conversion of around eleven percent of full sunlight into stored carbohydrate, with real vegetation achieving on the order of one percent averaged over a growing season and often far less over a year. Every subsequent biological step obeys the same discipline. When a caterpillar eats a leaf, when a bird eats the caterpillar, when bacteria decompose the bird, each transfer captures only a fraction of the energy on offer and degrades the rest to heat; metabolism itself, the maintenance of ion gradients, protein turnover, circulation, and movement, is a continuous tax paid in respiration. This is why energy pyramids narrow so relentlessly and why the total energy flowing through an ecosystem sets a hard ceiling on how much life, and what kinds of life, it can support. Thermodynamics is not background physics in ecology; it is the load-bearing wall.

sections.heading: Primary Production: Capturing the Sun
sections.body: The entry point of nearly all biological energy is primary production, the manufacture of organic compounds from carbon dioxide by autotrophs, the self-feeders: green plants on land, and in water the phytoplankton, algae, and cyanobacteria. Photosynthesis, summarized as carbon dioxide plus water, powered by light, yielding sugar and oxygen, stores about 479 kilojoules per mole of carbon fixed, and ecologists measure its output in grams of carbon, or dry biomass, per square meter per year. Vocabulary here does real work. Gross primary production, GPP, is the total carbon fixed. But plants are not passive collectors; they are working organisms that burn roughly half of their own gross production in respiration to build and maintain tissue. What remains, net primary production, NPP, equal to GPP minus plant respiration, is the biosphere's actual income, the energy embodied in new leaves, wood, roots, plankton cells, and seeds that is available to everything that eats. Global NPP is estimated at about 105 billion tonnes of carbon per year, split almost exactly half and half between land, about 56 billion tonnes, and ocean, about 49, a symmetry with a twist: the ocean achieves its half with a standing crop of photosynthesizers hundreds of times smaller than the land's, about one billion tonnes of phytoplankton versus several hundred billion tonnes of land plants, because phytoplankton are eaten and replaced within days while a tree stands for a century. Turnover, not standing stock, is what feeds food webs. What limits production? On land, first water and temperature: the map of NPP is essentially a map of rainfall and warmth, which is why tropical rainforest produces around 2,200 grams of dry matter per square meter per year while deserts manage under 90 and tundra around 140. Light matters at high latitude, and everywhere nutrients set the finer grain, especially nitrogen in temperate systems and phosphorus in many tropical soils. In the ocean, light restricts photosynthesis to the sunlit euphotic zone, roughly the top 50 to 200 meters, and nutrients dominate everything else: the vast central gyres are blue deserts because the thermocline seals nutrient-rich deep water away from the light, while coastal upwelling zones off Peru, California, and northwest Africa, where wind drags surface water aside and cold deep water rises, are among the most productive waters on Earth and yield a wildly disproportionate share of the world fish catch. In iron-poor regions of the Southern Ocean and equatorial Pacific, iron itself is limiting, demonstrated by experiments in the 1990s in which dissolving a few hundred kilograms of iron sulfate into the sea bloomed phytoplankton across hundreds of square kilometers, confirming John Martin's iron hypothesis. Methods of measurement have their own history: light-and-dark bottle oxygen incubations in water, harvest methods in grasslands, eddy-flux towers breathing with whole forests, and since the 1980s satellites converting ocean color and land greenness into global production maps, the source of most numbers in this section.

sections.heading: Life Without Light: Chemosynthesis
sections.body: Sunlight is the biosphere's overwhelming power source, but it is not the only one, and the exceptions are scientifically profound. Certain bacteria and archaea practice chemosynthesis, extracting energy not from photons but from chemical reactions between reduced inorganic compounds and an oxidant, usually oxygen, and using that energy to fix carbon dioxide into organic matter exactly as plants do. The classic energy sources are hydrogen sulfide, ammonia, hydrogen gas, ferrous iron, and methane. Nitrifying bacteria in every soil oxidize ammonia to nitrite and nitrate for energy; iron bacteria stain streambeds orange; sulfur oxidizers thrive wherever sulfide meets oxygen, in salt marshes, sewage outfalls, and cave systems such as Romania's Movile Cave, sealed for millions of years, whose entire food web rests on chemosynthetic films. For most of scientific history these organisms were regarded as a biochemical curiosity, minor players supported by geological leftovers. That changed abruptly in February 1977, when the submersible Alvin, diving on the Galapagos Rift 2,500 meters down to study seafloor spreading, found hot springs surrounded by dense thickets of life in what should have been near-barren abyss: giant tube worms two meters long, beds of clams and mussels, crabs, fish, all in total darkness. The energy source proved to be hydrogen sulfide in the vent fluid, oxidized by bacteria that either coat surfaces or, most remarkably, live inside the animals. The tube worm Riftia pachyptila has no mouth and no gut; a specialized organ called the trophosome is packed with symbiotic sulfur-oxidizing bacteria, and the worm's blood, red with a special hemoglobin that carries sulfide and oxygen simultaneously without poisoning itself, delivers the reactants to its tenants and lives on their products. Whole communities, hundreds of species new to science, are powered this way at hydrothermal vents along mid-ocean ridges, and a gentler analogue thrives at cold seeps, where methane and sulfide leak from continental margins and support tube worms estimated to live over two centuries. Whale falls, the carcasses of great whales on the deep seafloor, host a final chemosynthetic stage in which bacteria mine the sulfide generated by decomposing bones, and stepping-stone communities of specialized animals move between carcasses. Two honest caveats keep the picture accurate. First, chemosynthesis at vents is not fully independent of the sun today, because the oxygen the bacteria use as oxidant is a product of photosynthesis in the surface ocean; a truly light-independent biosphere exists only in rock-hosted microbial ecosystems running on hydrogen and buried oxidants, and such deep biosphere life, though vast in total mass, metabolizes extraordinarily slowly. Second, the global energy contribution of chemosynthesis is tiny beside photosynthesis, well under one percent. Its importance is conceptual: it proves that ecosystems require an energy gradient, not sunlight specifically, which is why the ice-covered oceans of Europa and Enceladus, with rocky seafloors and possible hydrothermal activity, are the solar system's most seriously discussed candidates for life beyond Earth.

sections.heading: Trophic Levels and Food Chains
sections.body: Once energy is fixed into living tissue, it moves by the oldest transaction in nature: something eats something else. Ecologists organize the traffic into trophic levels, from the Greek trophe, nourishment. Level one is the primary producers, the plants and phytoplankton. Level two is the primary consumers, herbivores, from aphids and zooplankton to elephants. Level three is the secondary consumers, carnivores that eat herbivores, and level four the tertiary consumers that eat other carnivores; a chain that runs grass to grasshopper to shrew to owl has four levels, and the owl sits at the top. Omnivores, humans included, feed at more than one level at once, and many animals change level over a lifetime: a freshwater perch begins life eating algae-grazing zooplankton and ends it eating fish that eat zooplankton, climbing a full level as it grows. Alongside the living, or grazing, chain runs the detrital chain, rooted not in green leaves but in dead organic matter, and carrying, in most ecosystems, the majority of all energy flow. Parasites form yet another set of feeding links, so numerous that in some estuarine food webs their combined biomass exceeds that of the top predators. The central empirical fact about food chains is that they are short. Most run three or four links; five is uncommon; chains of six or more occur mainly in open oceans, where a chain might run phytoplankton to copepod to krill to small fish to squid to tuna. Why so short? The classical answer, formalized by Lindeman in 1942, is energetic attrition: if only around a tenth of the energy at one level reaches the next, then a producer base of 10,000 units supports 1,000 units of herbivore, 100 of first-order carnivore, 10 of second-order, and a single unit two levels above that, and at some point there is simply too little energy flux to sustain a viable population of anything higher. The hypothesis predicts that more productive ecosystems should support longer chains, which holds only weakly in comparative data; ecosystem size and stability appear to matter as well, since long chains amplify fluctuations, and disturbance-prone systems favor short ones. Whatever the exact weighting of causes, the consequence is architectural: the top of the pyramid is thin, top predators are few, wide-ranging, and slow to reproduce, and they are therefore the first losses when ecosystems degrade. A practical corollary reaches the dinner table: a person fed on grain draws on roughly a tenth of the primary production that the same person fed on grain-fattened beef requires, which is why feeding the world's livestock takes several times the cropland that would feed its humans directly, and why fisheries that target tuna and swordfish are mining the sparse apex of a very tall marine pyramid.

sections.heading: Food Webs: The Real Architecture
sections.body: The food chain is a teaching diagram; the reality in any ecosystem is a web, a network in which dozens to thousands of species are connected by feeding links, most species eat and are eaten by several others, and energy finds many parallel routes from plants to apex predators. Charles Elton sketched the first such webs for Bear Island in the Arctic in the 1920s, and the modern, well-resolved versions, such as the web compiled for the Little Rock Lake system in Wisconsin with nearly two hundred taxa and over two thousand feeding links, are objects of network science as much as natural history. Their statistics show regularities: the fraction of possible links actually realized, called connectance, typically falls between 0.05 and 0.3; the average path from any species to any other is short, about two links, the small-world property; and webs are interval and modular, organized into loose compartments, often along habitat boundaries, that limit how far disturbances propagate. Within the tangle, certain structural motifs recur and matter. Keystone species, a term coined by Robert Paine in 1969 from his experiments on Washington State shores, are species whose influence is wildly out of proportion to their abundance: when Paine removed the predatory sea star Pisaster from experimental plots, the mussel it preyed on blanketed the rock and species richness collapsed from fifteen to eight, because the predator had been holding open space for weaker competitors. Ecosystem engineers, such as beavers, earthworms, and reef-building corals, restructure the physical habitat itself and thereby rewire the web around them. Basal resources and their consumers form the wide floor; a few super-generalist consumers act as hubs whose loss fragments the network, an insight borrowed directly from studies of internet robustness: simulations of real food webs show they tolerate random species loss fairly well but come apart quickly when the most connected species are deleted preferentially. Webs also blur the neat trophic-level scheme, and ecologists quantify the blur by assigning each species a fractional trophic level, one plus the weighted mean of its prey's levels, computed from diet data or from the stepwise enrichment of the heavy nitrogen isotope, which rises about three to four parts per thousand per trophic step and lets a tissue sample reveal where an animal really feeds. By this measure most terrestrial carnivores sit near level three to four, large tunas and billfish near four to five, and humans, calculated by Sylvain Bonhommeau and colleagues in 2013 from global diet statistics, average a modest 2.21, about the trophic level of a pig or an anchovy, though national averages range from near-vegetarian 2.0 to fish-and-meat-heavy 2.6. Two web-wide energy insights close the picture: omnivory and web loops spread risk, letting consumers switch prey as abundances shift, which is stabilizing; and most links are weak, with a few strong interactions embedded in a matrix of weak ones, an arrangement theory identifies as the reason rich, tangled communities do not simply oscillate themselves to pieces.

sections.heading: Ecological Efficiency and the Ten Percent Rule
sections.body: Between any two trophic levels stands a gauntlet of losses, and quantifying them is the core craft of production ecology. Follow the energy in a leaf that a caterpillar might eat. First, most of the leaf crop is never eaten at all; in a temperate forest, herbivores consume perhaps five to ten percent of net primary production while the rest falls to the decomposers, though on grazed savanna consumption can exceed half. What is eaten is not all digested: of the energy ingested, a share, often forty to sixty percent for a leaf-eater, passes through unassimilated as feces, giving an assimilation efficiency of forty to sixty percent for herbivores, seventy to ninety percent for carnivores eating easily digested flesh, and as low as twenty to thirty percent for detritivores chewing refractory litter. Of what is assimilated, most is burned in respiration, the cost of staying alive, and only the remainder becomes new tissue or offspring; this production efficiency varies enormously with physiology. Endotherms, the warm-blooded birds and mammals that pay a continuous heating bill, convert only about one to three percent of assimilated energy into growth; ectotherms such as insects, fish, and reptiles manage ten to forty percent, and sedentary aquatic invertebrates do best of all. Multiply the three fractions, consumption, assimilation, and production, and you have the trophic transfer efficiency, the percentage of one level's production that becomes the next level's production. Lindeman guessed about ten percent, and a famous compilation of forty-eight aquatic ecosystems by Pauly and Christensen in 1995 found a mean close to ten percent with a spread of roughly two to twenty-four, so the ten percent rule is a genuine central tendency with honest scatter, and terrestrial endotherm-dominated links often run well below it. The consequences compound geometrically. In the open ocean, where transfer efficiency runs near ten percent and chains are long, producing one kilogram of tuna at trophic level 4.5 requires on the order of several thousand kilograms of phytoplankton production; in upwelling systems, where anchovies feed nearly on the phytoplankton itself, a kilogram of fish costs only tens of kilograms of production, which is why the Peruvian anchoveta fishery alone has landed over ten million tonnes in a good year, more than a tenth of the entire world catch. The same arithmetic prices human diets: grain fed to cattle returns roughly three to five percent of its calories as beef, ten to fifteen percent as pork, around ten to twenty as chicken and eggs, and better than twenty as farmed carp or dairy, numbers that explain both the historical rarity of daily meat and the land hunger of modern livestock. Charles Elton put the whole subject in one sentence in 1927: animals at the base of a food chain are abundant, those at the end are few, and the progressive decrease in between is the fundamental fact of animal ecology.

sections.heading: Ecological Pyramids: Energy, Biomass, and Numbers
sections.body: The compounding of transfer losses gives ecosystems a characteristic shape, first drawn by Charles Elton in 1927 and now taught as the ecological pyramid, but the shape depends critically on what is being stacked, and the differences are instructive rather than pedantic. A pyramid of energy stacks the productivity of each trophic level, in units such as kilojoules per square meter per year, and it is the only pyramid that physics guarantees can never be inverted: each level's production is manufactured from the level below within the same period, so it must be smaller, and typically each bar is about an order of magnitude shorter than the one beneath. Howard Odum's meticulous budget of Silver Springs, Florida, in the 1950s made the canonical example: roughly 20,800 kilojoules per square meter per year of gross production by the eelgrass and algae, about 3,370 reaching herbivores, 383 to first-level carnivores, and 21 to the top carnivores, with decomposers processing more than the herbivores did. A pyramid of biomass stacks standing stock, the mass of living tissue present at one moment, and it usually tapers too, but aquatic systems can flip it: in the English Channel and much of the open ocean the zooplankton and fish outweigh the phytoplankton on any given day, because the phytoplankton population, grazed to a thin standing crop, doubles every day or two while its consumers live for months or years. The inverted biomass pyramid is a signature of fast turnover at the base, a demonstration that flow, not stock, feeds the web, and recent surveys of near-pristine coral reefs report a related anomaly, predator-heavy fish communities sustained by mobile prey subsidies from surrounding waters and by the predators' slow metabolism and long lives. A pyramid of numbers, stacking head counts, is the least reliable of the three: a single oak tree, one producer, supports hundreds of thousands of herbivorous insects, inverting the bottom, and parasite-rich webs invert at the top, because each host carries many small parasites; numbers pyramids mislead whenever body sizes differ sharply between levels, which is nearly always. At planetary scale the biomass census assembled by Yinon Bar-On, Rob Phillips, and Ron Milo in 2018 gives the pyramid its grandest expression: of roughly 550 billion tonnes of carbon in living things, plants hold about 450, bacteria around 70, fungi about 12, and the whole animal kingdom only about 2, within which arthropods and fish dominate, livestock outweigh wild mammals roughly twentyfold, and wild mammals total a mere 0.007 billion tonnes, about two percent of humanity's own mass. The pyramids also stack toxins in reverse: fat-soluble, slowly excreted substances such as methylmercury, DDT, and PCBs are not lost at each transfer as energy is, but concentrated, rising in tissue concentration by factors of millions from water to apex predator, which is why swordfish carry mercury advisories and why the pesticide-thinned eggshells of peregrine falcons and bald eagles made biomagnification a household word in the 1960s.

sections.heading: Decomposition and the Detrital Pathway
sections.body: The most heavily trafficked road in almost every ecosystem is the one nobody watches: the detrital pathway, along which dead organic matter, fallen leaves, wood, carcasses, feces, and the constant rain of dead plankton, is broken down and its energy and atoms recovered. In a typical forest, ninety percent or more of net primary production is never eaten alive; it dies in place and enters the detrital web, and even in grazed systems the feces of the grazers deliver much of the energy to the same destination. The workforce is layered by size. Scavengers and large detritivores, vultures, burying beetles, crabs, open carcasses and haul material about. The soil's mesofauna, earthworms, millipedes, woodlice, springtails, and mites in astonishing densities, tens of thousands of springtails can live beneath a single square meter of forest floor, shred litter into fragments, multiplying the surface area available to the true chemists: fungi and bacteria. Fungi, whose hyphae penetrate solid tissue and secrete enzymes that dismantle cellulose and, almost uniquely, lignin, the tough phenolic polymer of wood, dominate the decay of plant litter; white-rot basidiomycete fungi are essentially the only organisms that fully mineralize lignin, and the sixty-million-year lag between the evolution of woody plants and the (still debated) rise of efficient lignin-degrading fungi is one proposed reason the Carboniferous period buried so much unrotted carbon as coal. Bacteria dominate wet, low-oxygen, and animal-derived decay. The rate of the whole process is governed by a memorable trio, climate, quality, and organisms: decomposition roughly doubles with every ten degrees Celsius of warming, is throttled by both drought and waterlogging, since anaerobic decay is far slower and less complete, and depends on litter quality, indexed by the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio and lignin content. Fresh leaves with a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio near 25 to 1 vanish in months; straw at 80 to 1 lingers; resinous conifer needles and wood persist for years to decades. In consequence, a tropical rainforest leaf may decompose in weeks and the forest stores most of its carbon in living biomass above thin soils, while cold peatlands decompose so slowly that thousands of years of production accumulate as peat, and the permafrost region has banked on the order of 1,500 billion tonnes of soil carbon, roughly twice the carbon content of the entire atmosphere, a stock now beginning to thaw. Decomposition's end state is twofold: mineralization, the release of carbon dioxide and of nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur in inorganic forms that plants can reuse, closing the nutrient loops, and humification, the formation of dark, chemically recalcitrant soil organic matter that can persist for centuries and gives fertile soils their color and water-holding capacity. The detrital web is thus simultaneously the biosphere's recycling plant and its savings bank, and no account of energy flow balances without it: in Odum's Silver Springs budget, more energy passed through the decomposers than through all animal consumers combined.

sections.heading: The Carbon Cycle: Energy's Material Shadow
sections.body: Because the energy of ecosystems is stored in carbon compounds, the flow of energy and the cycle of carbon are two views of one machine, and the carbon numbers deserve to be known outright. The atmosphere holds about 880 billion tonnes of carbon as carbon dioxide, a figure rising by roughly 5 billion tonnes a year; the living and dead organic matter of land ecosystems holds around 2,300 billion, two thirds of it in soils rather than vegetation; the surface ocean and deep ocean together hold about 38,000 billion, mostly as dissolved inorganic bicarbonate; and sedimentary rocks hold millions of billions, the slow geological reservoir. The annual fluxes dwarf human intuition: terrestrial photosynthesis draws down about 120 billion tonnes of carbon each year, and respiration by plants, animals, and, mostly, decomposer microbes returns almost exactly as much; the ocean exchanges about 90 billion tonnes a year with the atmosphere across its surface. These vast opposing flows are why atmospheric carbon dioxide breathes seasonally, falling through the northern summer as the great land masses photosynthesize and rising through winter, the sawtooth visible in the Keeling curve recorded continuously at Mauna Loa since 1958. Within ecosystems, ecologists extend the production vocabulary one step: net ecosystem production, NEP, is net primary production minus the respiration of all the heterotrophs, and it measures whether a whole ecosystem is accumulating carbon, a sink, or releasing it, a source. A young, regrowing forest has strongly positive NEP; an old-growth forest hovers near balance while storing an enormous standing stock; a drained peatland or a burning one is a fierce source. Two biological pumps move carbon against gradients. On land, the yearly conveyor from leaf to litter to soil builds the soil carbon bank. At sea, the biological pump exports carbon from the sunlit layer as dead cells, fecal pellets, and vertical migrations carry organic matter into the deep; only a fraction of a percent reaches the sediments, but the pump maintains a deep-ocean carbon store that would otherwise equilibrate with the surface, and without it atmospheric carbon dioxide would be on the order of 150 to 200 parts per million higher. Human combustion of fossil fuels and cement production now inject about 10 billion tonnes of carbon per year, with land clearing adding roughly another one; about half stays in the atmosphere, a quarter dissolves into the ocean, acidifying it measurably, and a quarter is being absorbed by land ecosystems, a subsidy from enhanced plant growth under higher carbon dioxide and recovering forests whose future strength is one of the genuine uncertainties of climate science. The carbon cycle is thus no longer a background loop; it is a lever humanity is actively pulling, and the direction of ecosystem energy flow research has shifted accordingly, from describing the machine to forecasting its feedbacks.

sections.heading: Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and the Law of the Minimum
sections.body: Energy may power ecosystems, but atoms constrain them, and two elements above all: nitrogen and phosphorus. The principle governing their influence is Justus von Liebig's law of the minimum, articulated for crop fields in 1840: growth is limited not by the total of resources available but by the single resource in shortest supply relative to need. Living tissue requires elements in roughly fixed proportions, and marine plankton are so consistent that the ratio bears a name, the Redfield ratio, discovered by Alfred Redfield in 1934: 106 atoms of carbon to 16 of nitrogen to 1 of phosphorus, a stoichiometry so pervasive that deviations from it are used to diagnose which nutrient limits a given sea. Nitrogen is the great paradox: the atmosphere is seventy-eight percent nitrogen gas, yet the triple bond of the dinitrogen molecule is so strong that no plant or animal can use it. Entry into the living world runs almost entirely through biological nitrogen fixation, performed only by certain bacteria and archaea wielding the enzyme nitrogenase, at a metabolic cost of about sixteen molecules of ATP per molecule of nitrogen fixed; the most celebrated fixers, Rhizobium bacteria, live in root nodules of legumes, trading ammonia for sugar, which is why clover, beans, and alfalfa enrich soil and anchor crop rotations, and why cyanobacteria such as Trichodesmium play the same role at sea. Lightning fixes a few percent more.
