Cascades run through behavior as much as through killing, the ecology of fear: prey under predation risk feed less, in worse places, and reproduce more slowly, so a predator's mere presence can suppress herbivory without a single additional kill. Cascades also run bottom-up, since adding nutrients or light expands every level from below, and ecosystems are shaped by the perpetual tension between the two directions; whole-lake experiments by Stephen Carpenter and James Kitchell in the 1980s showed that manipulating top fish predators shifted algal biomass dramatically even while nutrient loading set the stage, a finding applied practically as biomanipulation, restoring clear water to eutrophic lakes by managing fish to favor grazing zooplankton. The applied lesson cuts both ways. Removing apex predators triggers mesopredator release, the explosion of mid-sized predators like coyotes, rats, or small sharks once their enemies vanish, with cascading damage to songbirds, seabirds, and shellfish; overfishing Atlantic cod off Nova Scotia released forage fish and crustaceans, delaying cod recovery for decades. Restoring predators, conversely, is now understood not as sentiment but as infrastructure repair: an intact top of the pyramid stabilizes the levels below, dampens outbreaks, and can even alter disease transmission and carbon budgets. The pyramid is not a static diagram; it is a control system, and its top floors are load-bearing.

sections.heading: Limits of the Ten Percent Rule, and How To Use It Well
sections.body: Every powerful simplification invites misuse, and the energy pyramid deserves confidence only within marked boundaries. First, ten percent is a central tendency, not a law of nature. Measured trophic transfer efficiencies span from below 2 percent in many terrestrial and endotherm-dominated links to 30 percent or more in cold-blooded plankton chains, and the compilation behind the famous average revealed that spread; using ten percent for a specific ecosystem without checking its physiology and structure can be wrong by an order of magnitude. Second, trophic levels are a discretization of a web that is genuinely continuous: omnivory, diet shifts with age, cannibalism, and parasitism smear organisms across fractional levels, so professionals increasingly work with isotope-based trophic positions such as 3.4 rather than integer rungs, and the pyramid should be read as a flow summary, not an org chart of nature. Third, snapshots deceive: pyramids of numbers invert under a single oak, pyramids of biomass invert over the ocean's fast-spinning plankton, and only the pyramid of energy flux is guaranteed upright, so any argument built on standing stocks rather than flows is vulnerable to turnover effects. Fourth, the diagrams traditionally omit the majority channel, the detrital web, and ignore subsidies between ecosystems, the tidal export that feeds coastal waters from salt marshes, the salmon that carry ocean energy far upstream into forests, the insects that rain from streamside trees into rivers; real budgets leak across boundaries that diagrams draw as walls. Fifth, energy is not the only currency that structures ecosystems: nitrogen, phosphorus, iron, and water limit production in many places, ecological stoichiometry shows that consumers can be constrained by nutrient ratios even amid caloric plenty, and information, behavior, fear, learning, migration, steers flows in ways pure energetics cannot predict. Sixth, the pyramid is not stationary under human pressure: warming raises metabolic costs for ectotherms roughly exponentially, with respiration outpacing photosynthesis in many models of warming seas, implying thinner future transfers; fishing and hunting have preferentially removed the apex, shortening chains; nutrient pollution swells the base until decomposition consumes the oxygen, producing the Gulf of Mexico and Baltic dead zones; and fossil-fueled agriculture props a temporary extra story under one species. Knowing this, use the framework where it is strong. It will tell you, reliably, why big fierce animals are rare, in Paul Colinvaux's phrase; why a hectare feeds more vegetarians than carnivores; why persistent fat-soluble toxins belong in the fewest possible fish advisories at the highest levels; why draining, damming, or clearing the productive base decapitates food chains from the top; and why any scheme, ecological or agricultural, that promises to insert extra conversion steps without cost is arithmetic dressed as innovation. Where you need precision, reach for the real tools, measured NPP, system-specific efficiencies, isotope positions, mass-balance models, and treat every round number as a hypothesis. The pyramid's deepest teaching survives every caveat: life runs on a one-way river of solar energy, every feeding step pays a steep thermodynamic toll, and the architecture of the living world, from the greenness of continents to the emptiness of the open sea's upper stories, is the visible shape of that toll being paid.

guides.title: Primary Productivity in Ecosystems
guides.summary: How living systems capture energy from sunlight and chemistry, what limits the rate, and how productivity is measured on land and at sea. Covers the biochemistry, the global pattern, the controls, the human appropriation of it, and how the numbers are actually obtained.

sections.heading: What primary productivity is and why everything depends on it
sections.body:
Primary productivity is the rate at which living organisms convert energy from an external source, almost always sunlight, into the chemical bonds of organic matter. It is a rate, not a stock, and the distinction is the first thing to get right. Biomass is how much organic material is standing there at a given moment, measured in grams of carbon per square metre. Productivity is how fast new organic matter is being made, measured in grams of carbon per square metre per year. A mature forest holds enormous biomass and may add rather little each year; a patch of ocean holds almost no standing biomass yet turns it over so rapidly that its annual production rivals a grassland's.

Two terms partition the flow. Gross primary production, GPP, is the total amount of carbon fixed by photosynthesis. Plants then respire, burning some of that carbon to power their own metabolism - protein synthesis, ion transport, tissue maintenance, growth. Net primary production, NPP, is what remains: GPP minus autotrophic respiration. NPP is the quantity that matters ecologically, because it is the energy actually available to everything that cannot photosynthesise. Across the biosphere, autotrophic respiration consumes roughly half of GPP, so NPP is on the order of 50 per cent of gross fixation, though the fraction varies from about 30 per cent in old forests with large respiring woody tissue to perhaps 60 to 70 per cent in fast-growing crops and phytoplankton.

A third term extends the accounting to the whole system. Net ecosystem production, NEP, subtracts heterotrophic respiration - the decomposition carried out by animals, fungi and bacteria - from NPP. NEP is what determines whether an ecosystem is accumulating carbon or releasing it, and it can be negative in a system where decomposition of previously stored material exceeds current fixation, as when a drained peatland oxidises soil carbon laid down over millennia.

The reason this quantity organises ecology is that it sets the energy budget for everything else. Every herbivore, predator, decomposer and parasite is ultimately living on the carbon that primary producers fixed. Because energy transfer between trophic levels is inefficient, typically 10 per cent with a realistic range of 2 to 20 per cent, the amount of production at the base determines how many trophic levels a system can support and how much biomass can exist at each. A system fixing 2,000 grams of carbon per square metre per year can support a food web that one fixing 20 simply cannot.

It also sets the terms of human existence. All food, all fossil fuel, all fibre and timber is stored or current primary production. The global scale is worth holding in mind: roughly 100 to 120 petagrams of carbon per year of terrestrial GPP, and about 50 to 60 petagrams of NPP on land with a comparable amount in the ocean. A petagram is a billion tonnes.

sections.heading: The biochemistry: how carbon is actually fixed
sections.body:
Photosynthesis is conventionally split into two coupled sets of reactions. The light reactions, in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts, use absorbed photons to strip electrons from water, releasing oxygen as a by-product, and use the resulting electron flow to pump protons and generate ATP and NADPH. Two photosystems operate in series - photosystem II, which oxidises water and absorbs most strongly near 680 nanometres, and photosystem I, absorbing near 700 nanometres - connected by an electron transport chain. The energetic requirement is substantial: roughly eight photons per molecule of carbon dioxide fixed under ideal conditions, which places a hard ceiling on efficiency.

The carbon reactions, the Calvin-Benson cycle, use that ATP and NADPH to attach carbon dioxide to a five-carbon sugar, ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, producing two three-carbon molecules that are reduced to sugars, with most of the flow recycled to regenerate the acceptor. The enzyme responsible, ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase, universally called RuBisCO, is almost certainly the most abundant protein on Earth, plausibly 0.7 billion tonnes globally, and it is remarkably bad at its job. It is slow, fixing perhaps 3 to 10 carbon dioxide molecules per second per active site where a typical enzyme manages thousands, which forces plants to synthesise enormous quantities of it - often 20 to 30 per cent of leaf nitrogen. Worse, it cannot cleanly distinguish carbon dioxide from oxygen. When it binds oxygen instead, it initiates photorespiration, a salvage pathway that consumes energy and releases previously fixed carbon, wasting perhaps 20 to 30 per cent of potential production in warm conditions.

This flaw is an accident of history. RuBisCO evolved when the atmosphere held almost no oxygen and far more carbon dioxide, and the discrimination problem only became costly after oxygenic photosynthesis itself transformed the atmosphere. Because the enzyme sits at the centre of a metabolism with countless dependencies, evolution has been unable to redesign it, and has instead evolved workarounds.

The most important workaround is C4 photosynthesis, which evolved independently more than sixty times, largely within the last 30 million years as atmospheric carbon dioxide fell. C4 plants first fix carbon using PEP carboxylase, an enzyme with no affinity for oxygen, into a four-carbon acid in mesophyll cells. That acid is shuttled into specialised bundle sheath cells where it is decarboxylated, concentrating carbon dioxide around RuBisCO to perhaps ten times ambient and largely suppressing photorespiration. The cost is extra ATP, which makes C4 advantageous in hot, bright, dry conditions and disadvantageous in cool or shaded ones. Maize, sugarcane, sorghum and most tropical grasses are C4; wheat, rice and trees are C3. CAM plants, including cacti and agaves, solve the same problem temporally, opening stomata at night to capture carbon dioxide as malate and processing it by day with stomata shut, trading productivity for extreme water efficiency.

sections.heading: The efficiency ceiling: why plants capture so little sunlight
sections.body:
Photosynthesis is often described as remarkably efficient, and at the level of a single reaction centre converting an absorbed photon into a separated charge it genuinely is, exceeding 90 per cent. At the level of a whole crop turning incident sunlight into harvestable biomass, it is not. Tracing where the energy goes is one of the most clarifying exercises in the subject.

Start with 100 per cent of solar energy at the top of a canopy. Only about 48 to 50 per cent falls in the 400 to 700 nanometre band that photosynthetic pigments can use, the photosynthetically active radiation; the infrared, which carries most of the rest, cannot drive the reactions. Of that, a canopy reflects and transmits perhaps 10 per cent, leaving roughly 43 per cent absorbed. Converting absorbed photons to carbohydrate carries an unavoidable thermodynamic and quantum cost, since a red photon carries more energy than is stored and blue photons are degraded to the red level before use; this leaves about 37 per cent as the theoretical maximum energy captured in carbohydrate. Photorespiration in a C3 plant at present carbon dioxide levels and 30 degrees Celsius removes about a further 6.1 percentage points. Plant respiration then consumes 30 to 60 per cent of what remains.

The arithmetic, worked through carefully by Robert Blankenship, Xin-Guang Zhu, Stephen Long and colleagues, gives a theoretical maximum of about 4.6 per cent for C3 plants and 6.0 per cent for C4 plants. Real crops fall well short. The best short-term field performance, for sugarcane or miscanthus under ideal conditions, reaches 2 to 3 per cent. Annual averages for well-managed temperate crops are 0.5 to 1.5 per cent, and the global average across all land vegetation is around 0.3 per cent, because most land is limited by water, nutrients, temperature or season length for most of the year.

This ceiling has direct practical consequences that are often missed in energy debates. It explains why bioenergy requires so much land: a photovoltaic panel converts 15 to 22 per cent of incident sunlight to electricity, roughly an order of magnitude better than the best crop, and considerably more than that against a realistic annual average. It explains why the theoretical yield ceiling of a crop is a real biophysical limit rather than a failure of effort, and why plant breeding gains since the Green Revolution have come mostly from harvest index - the fraction of biomass in grain rather than straw - and from extending the duration of light interception, rather than from improving photosynthetic efficiency itself. Harvest index in wheat rose from around 0.3 to nearly 0.5 over the twentieth century, and that particular well is close to dry, which is why efforts have turned to engineering photosynthesis directly.

sections.heading: What limits production on land: water, warmth, light and nutrients
sections.body:
Terrestrial productivity is jointly controlled by a small number of factors, and which one binds determines almost everything about a landscape's ecology. The general principle is Liebig's law of the minimum, articulated by Justus von Liebig in the 1840s: growth is governed by the scarcest necessary resource, not by the total supply of all of them. Adding nitrogen to a drought-stricken system does nothing.

Water is the dominant control across most of the land surface. The relationship between annual precipitation and NPP is close to linear across the dry end of the range, roughly 0.4 to 0.6 grams of carbon per square metre per millimetre of rain, until it saturates somewhere above 2,000 to 2,500 millimetres per year. The mechanism is a direct physical trade-off at the leaf surface: carbon dioxide enters through stomata, and water vapour leaves through the same pores. A plant cannot acquire carbon without losing water, and the exchange rate is brutal - a C3 plant typically transpires 400 to 700 grams of water per gram of dry matter produced, a C4 plant 200 to 350. Water-use efficiency is therefore not a peripheral trait but the central axis of plant strategy in most of the world.

Temperature controls production through enzyme kinetics and through season length. Photosynthesis in temperate species typically peaks between 20 and 30 degrees Celsius and declines above that as photorespiration rises and, at higher temperatures still, as membranes and proteins destabilise. In cold biomes the binding constraint is usually the length of the frost-free growing season rather than the instantaneous rate: an arctic sedge may photosynthesise perfectly well but has only sixty days in which to do it.

Nutrients bind where water and warmth are adequate. Nitrogen is generally limiting in temperate and boreal systems, because it enters ecosystems mainly through biological fixation and is easily lost by leaching and denitrification, and because RuBisCO and chlorophyll are nitrogen-expensive. Phosphorus is generally limiting in old, highly weathered tropical soils, because its ultimate source is rock and millions of years of weathering have depleted and locked it into unavailable iron and aluminium compounds. This is the resolution of an old puzzle: lush tropical rainforest often stands on soil that is nutritionally poor, because the nutrients are held in living biomass and cycled rapidly rather than stored in the ground, which is why clearing such forest yields only a few years of good cropping.

Light limits in dense canopies and understories. Leaf area index - square metres of leaf per square metre of ground - reaches 3 to 6 in most productive systems and 8 or more in some conifer forests, and light attenuates through a canopy approximately exponentially following the Beer-Lambert relationship. Below a certain depth a leaf costs more to maintain than it earns, and the plant sheds it, which sets canopy depth as an economic optimum rather than a fixed species trait.

sections.heading: The global pattern: which ecosystems produce most
sections.body:
Ranking ecosystems by productivity per unit area and by global total gives two different answers, and holding both in mind prevents most common misconceptions. The figures below are net primary production in grams of carbon per square metre per year, and should be read as central estimates with real uncertainty of perhaps 20 to 30 per cent.

At the top per unit area sit tropical rainforests at roughly 900 to 1,100, swamps and marshes at 900 to 1,200, tropical seasonal forests around 700 to 800, estuaries and coral reefs at 500 to 1,000, and intensively managed cropland around 300 to 600. In the middle come temperate deciduous forests at 500 to 700, temperate evergreen forests at 400 to 600, savanna at 300 to 500, and boreal forest at 200 to 300. At the bottom are temperate grassland at 200 to 350, tundra at 60 to 140, desert scrub at 30 to 90, extreme desert and ice at under 10, and the open ocean at roughly 100 to 150.

The open ocean number is the one that reliably surprises people. Per square metre the open sea is close to a desert, because the sunlit surface layer is separated from the nutrient-rich deep water by density stratification. Yet the ocean covers 71 per cent of the planet, and its total annual production, approximately 45 to 55 petagrams of carbon, roughly equals that of all land. Marine primary production is carried out overwhelmingly by microscopic phytoplankton whose total standing biomass is only about 1 to 2 petagrams of carbon, against roughly 450 to 500 for land plants. The ocean produces as much as the land from about one three-hundredth of the biomass, because phytoplankton turn over every few days while a tree stands for a century. This is the clearest possible demonstration that biomass and productivity are different quantities.

Turnover time, biomass divided by production, makes the point quantitatively: a few days for phytoplankton, one to three years for grassland including roots, and twenty to fifty years for forest biomass. It explains why marine systems respond to nutrient changes within a week while forests respond over decades.

Distribution on land follows water and temperature so closely that a map of NPP looks much like a map of climate. Production peaks in a band around the equator, collapses across the subtropical deserts near 20 to 30 degrees latitude where descending air suppresses rainfall, recovers in the temperate zone, and declines again toward the poles. Miami Beach's coastal wetlands and the Congo basin lie on the same productivity contour for entirely different reasons - one has abundant water and nutrients delivered by tides, the other abundant water, warmth and rapid internal cycling.

sections.heading: The ocean: nutrients, upwelling and the iron story
sections.body:
Marine primary production is limited by a different geometry from the land. Light penetrates only the upper ocean, with the euphotic zone conventionally defined as the depth to which 1 per cent of surface light reaches - about 100 to 200 metres in clear open water, 20 to 40 metres in productive coastal water, and sometimes only a few metres in turbid estuaries. Nutrients, meanwhile, are concentrated at depth, because sinking particles carry them downward and remineralisation releases them below the lit layer. Production therefore depends on physical processes that bring deep water up into the light.

Upwelling is the dominant such process. Along the eastern boundaries of ocean basins - off Peru and Chile, California, Namibia and Mauritania - equatorward winds combine with the Coriolis effect to drive surface water offshore through Ekman transport, and cold nutrient-rich water rises to replace it. These regions occupy under 1 per cent of the ocean surface yet historically supplied around 20 per cent of the world's fish catch. The Peruvian anchoveta fishery, the largest single-species fishery ever recorded, exists entirely because of this mechanism, and collapses during El Nino events when warm water caps the upwelling and the nutrient supply fails.

Other supply routes include seasonal deep mixing when winter cooling and storms break down stratification, riverine input of nitrogen and phosphorus, and atmospheric deposition of dust. The classic temperate spring bloom results from the interaction of two of these: winter mixing replenishes surface nutrients but also carries cells too deep to grow; when spring warming restratifies the surface, cells are held in the light with nutrients still abundant, and production explodes until the nutrients are exhausted.

The most interesting chapter concerns iron. Certain vast regions - the Southern Ocean, the equatorial Pacific, the subarctic Pacific - have abundant nitrate and phosphate yet low chlorophyll, a pattern named high-nutrient low-chlorophyll. John Martin proposed in the 1980s that the missing ingredient was iron, needed in trace amounts for the electron transport chain and for nitrate reduction, and supplied mainly by wind-blown continental dust which barely reaches those regions. His remark that giving him half a tanker of iron would let him give you an ice age became notorious. A series of open-ocean fertilisation experiments beginning with IronEx in 1993 and continuing through SOIREE, SOFeX and LOHAFEX confirmed the biological prediction emphatically: adding a few tonnes of iron sulphate triggered large blooms within days. Whether the carbon actually sinks and is sequestered for centuries proved far less clear, with most studies finding modest and variable export, and the approach as a climate intervention is now generally regarded as unproven and ecologically risky rather than promising.

sections.heading: Production without sunlight: chemosynthesis
sections.body:
Almost all primary production is powered by sunlight, but not quite all. Chemosynthetic organisms fix carbon using energy released by oxidising inorganic chemicals, and although they contribute a small fraction of the global total, they are of enormous theoretical importance and they support entire ecosystems that would otherwise be impossible.

The discovery was one of the genuine shocks of twentieth-century biology. In February 1977, the submersible Alvin, investigating the Galapagos Rift at about 2,500 metres depth, found dense communities of giant tube worms, clams and crabs clustered around hot vents in a region that should have been a nutritional desert - far below the reach of light, and receiving only the sparse rain of organic particles from above. The biomass density observed rivalled a tropical rainforest. The explanation, worked out over the following years, was that bacteria were oxidising hydrogen sulphide emerging from the vents and using the released energy to fix carbon dioxide, exactly as plants use light.

The chemistry is general. Sulphur-oxidising bacteria convert hydrogen sulphide to sulphate; nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonia to nitrite and nitrite to nitrate; iron-oxidising bacteria convert ferrous to ferric iron; methanotrophs oxidise methane; hydrogen-oxidising bacteria use hydrogen directly. Many of these organisms use the same Calvin-Benson cycle and the same RuBisCO enzyme as plants, simply supplying the ATP and reducing power from chemistry rather than photons. Others use alternative carbon fixation pathways - the reductive tricarboxylic acid cycle, the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway, the 3-hydroxypropionate cycle - of which at least six are now known, several considerably more energy-efficient than the Calvin cycle and probably far older.

The giant tube worm Riftia pachyptila is the emblematic case and is worth understanding in detail. It has no mouth, no gut and no anus as an adult. Instead it houses symbiotic sulphur-oxidising bacteria in a specialised organ, the trophosome, which may constitute half its body weight. Its plume, bright red from a specialised haemoglobin, binds oxygen and hydrogen sulphide simultaneously at separate sites - sulphide is normally a potent poison that blocks cytochrome c oxidase - and transports both to the bacteria. Growth rates exceeding 80 centimetres a year make it among the fastest-growing marine invertebrates known.

Chemosynthesis also matters for the deep subsurface biosphere, where microbial communities living in rock pores kilometres down subsist on hydrogen produced by radiolysis of water or by serpentinisation of ultramafic rock. Estimates of the total mass of this biosphere are genuinely uncertain, spanning perhaps 15 to 23 petagrams of carbon, but the metabolic rates are extraordinarily slow, with generation times possibly measured in centuries. The astrobiological significance is direct: chemosynthesis demonstrates that life does not require a star's light at the point of use, only a persistent chemical disequilibrium, which is why subsurface oceans on Europa and Enceladus are treated as plausible habitats.

sections.heading: Measuring production on land
sections.body:
Nothing in this field is measured directly. Every number for primary production is inferred from something else, and each method has characteristic biases that determine what its numbers can honestly be used for.

Harvest methods are the oldest and conceptually simplest: clip, dry and weigh the vegetation in a known area. They work well for annual crops and grasslands, where a single growing season's growth can be removed cleanly. They understate production systematically in three ways that are easy to forget. Belowground production is missed unless roots are excavated, and roots are commonly 30 to 70 per cent of NPP in grassland. Tissue that grew and died before harvest - shed leaves, fine roots turning over several times a season - is missed entirely. And material consumed by herbivores before harvest is invisible, which in a heavily grazed system can be a third of the total.

Forest inventory uses allometry. Measuring the diameter at breast height of every tree in a plot and applying species-specific equations relating diameter to biomass gives standing stock; repeating the census after several years gives increment. Litterfall traps capture leaf and twig production, and ingrowth cores or minirhizotrons estimate fine root turnover. The dominant uncertainty is usually the allometric equations, which are built from destructive sampling of relatively few trees and extrapolated widely, and errors of 20 to 30 per cent in large-tree biomass are common.

Eddy covariance, which became widespread from the 1990s and now underpins the global FLUXNET network of several hundred sites, measures the net exchange of carbon dioxide between an ecosystem and the atmosphere. A sonic anemometer and an infrared gas analyser mounted on a tower sample vertical wind speed and carbon dioxide concentration at 10 to 20 hertz; the covariance of the fluctuations gives net flux directly. It measures net ecosystem exchange continuously and non-destructively over a footprint of hundreds of metres. Its weaknesses are that it requires turbulent conditions - calm nights systematically underestimate respiration and require gap-filling with modelled values, a known bias - and that separating GPP from respiration requires assumptions rather than measurement.

Satellite remote sensing supplies the global picture. Chlorophyll absorbs strongly in the red and reflects strongly in the near infrared, and the normalised difference vegetation index exploits exactly that contrast, computed as the difference between near-infrared and red reflectance divided by their sum. NDVI saturates in dense canopies above a leaf area index of about 3, which limits it in rainforests, and the newer enhanced vegetation index and solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence partially address this. Fluorescence is particularly valuable because it is emitted by photosystem II during active photosynthesis, making it a signal of function rather than merely of greenness.

sections.heading: Measuring production in water
sections.body:
Aquatic measurement developed its own toolkit, and the classical methods remain instructive because they make the definitional distinctions physically tangible.

The light and dark bottle technique, developed in the 1920s and still used in teaching and fieldwork, is the clearest illustration of what GPP and NPP actually mean. Water is drawn from a chosen depth and divided among three bottles. One is analysed immediately for dissolved oxygen. The other two, one transparent and one wrapped to exclude all light, are suspended back at the sampling depth for a known period, typically four to twenty-four hours, then analysed. In the light bottle both photosynthesis and respiration proceed, so the oxygen change gives net community production. In the dark bottle only respiration occurs, so the oxygen decrease gives community respiration. Adding the two gives gross production. Converting from oxygen to carbon requires a photosynthetic quotient, usually taken as 1.2 moles of oxygen released per mole of carbon fixed, which is an assumption rather than a measurement and varies with the nitrogen source used.

The carbon-14 method, introduced by Einer Steemann Nielsen in 1952, transformed oceanography by being far more sensitive. A trace of radioactive bicarbonate is added to a sample, which is incubated, then filtered; the radioactivity retained on the filter, scaled by the ratio of labelled to total inorganic carbon, gives carbon fixed. Its sensitivity allows measurement in the open ocean where oxygen changes would be undetectable. Its persistent ambiguity is that, depending on incubation length, the result falls somewhere between gross and net production, because some labelled carbon is respired during the incubation. Short incubations approach GPP, long ones approach NPP, and the literature contains decades of argument about the comparability of published numbers as a result.

Modern approaches include stable isotope methods using oxygen-18 labelled water, fast repetition rate fluorometry which infers photosynthetic electron transport from the fluorescence response to rapid flash sequences without any incubation at all, and in-situ oxygen optodes on autonomous floats and gliders that resolve daily production cycles across whole ocean basins.

Satellite ocean colour provides the global synthesis. Sensors from the Coastal Zone Color Scanner in 1978 through SeaWiFS, MODIS and the current generation estimate surface chlorophyll from water-leaving radiance in blue and green bands. Chlorophyll is then converted to production through models such as Behrenfeld and Falkowski's vertically generalised production model, which combines chlorophyll, available light, sea surface temperature and euphotic depth. These estimates carry substantial uncertainty - different algorithms applied to the same satellite data can differ by a factor approaching two in some regions - and only see the surface layer, missing deep chlorophyll maxima that can hold a significant fraction of total production.

sections.heading: From production to food webs: trophic transfer
sections.body:
Primary production sets the budget, but only a fraction of it reaches any given consumer, and the accounting of those losses explains much about how ecosystems are structured.

Ecological efficiency, the proportion of energy at one trophic level that appears at the next, averages around 10 per cent with a realistic range of roughly 2 to 20 per cent. The figure is often quoted as a law and is better understood as a rough empirical average of three separate efficiencies multiplied together. Consumption efficiency is the fraction of available production actually eaten - very low in forests, where perhaps 1 to 10 per cent of leaf production is consumed alive because wood and mature leaves are indigestible and defended, but 20 to 50 per cent in grasslands and often above 50 per cent in plankton systems where cells are small, soft and undefended. Assimilation efficiency is the fraction of ingested material absorbed rather than excreted - roughly 20 to 50 per cent for herbivores eating cellulose-rich plants, and 60 to 90 per cent for carnivores eating flesh, which is chemically much more similar to the consumer's own tissue. Production efficiency is the fraction of assimilated energy converted to new consumer biomass rather than burned in respiration, and this is where the endotherm penalty appears: mammals and birds convert only 1 to 3 per cent, because maintaining body temperature is metabolically ruinous, while insects manage 30 to 40 per cent and fish around 10 per cent.

Multiplying these explains why a food chain rarely exceeds four or five levels. Starting from 1,000 units of plant production, a 10 per cent transfer gives 100 to herbivores, 10 to primary carnivores, 1 to secondary carnivores. A fifth level would live on 0.1 units, which cannot sustain a viable population of anything large. Chain length is limited by energy, and secondarily by the instability that long chains exhibit.

This also explains the shapes of ecological pyramids and one important exception. A pyramid of energy is always broad at the base, because energy is genuinely lost at each step and thermodynamics forbids otherwise. A pyramid of biomass usually is too, but in open-ocean plankton systems it inverts: the standing biomass of zooplankton can exceed that of the phytoplankton they eat, because the phytoplankton reproduce so fast that a small standing crop supports a large consumer population. The pyramid of energy for the same system remains upright. Any apparent violation is a confusion of stock with flow.

The practical consequence for human diets follows directly. Producing a kilogram of beef requires roughly 25 kilograms of feed and 15,000 litres of water; a kilogram of chicken roughly 4.5 kilograms of feed. Eating at a lower trophic level captures more of the underlying primary production, which is why the land footprint of diets varies by an order of magnitude.

sections.heading: A field protocol: estimating grassland net primary production
sections.body:
The peak-standing-crop harvest method is the most accessible way to obtain a real productivity number, and working through it teaches the biases better than reading about them. It suits herbaceous vegetation with a single annual growth cycle and is unsuitable for shrubland or forest. The output is aboveground net primary production in grams of dry matter per square metre per year, convertible to carbon by multiplying by about 0.45 to 0.48.

The logic is that where the entire shoot dies back each winter, the mass standing at peak growth approximates one season's production. Every deviation from that idealisation biases the answer downward: grazing losses, early-season mortality, and everything below ground. In grassland root production usually exceeds shoot production, so an aboveground figure is never total NPP.

Timing governs quality more than any other choice, and replication runs it close: grassland biomass is patchy, coefficients of variation of 20 to 40 per cent between quadrats are normal, and a single quadrat yields a number with no defensible precision. Interpret the result against published ranges - roughly 200 to 350 grams of carbon per square metre per year for temperate grassland total NPP.
ingredients: A quadrat frame of known area, commonly 0.25 square metres (50 by 50 centimetres) or 1 square metre, in rigid pipe, timber or rod. Measure its internal area rather than assuming it.
Sharp shears or grass scissors that cut cleanly at ground level without uprooting.
Paper bags or envelopes for each sample; plastic traps moisture and encourages mould before drying.
A drying oven holding 60 to 70 degrees Celsius. Do not exceed about 80 degrees, which volatilises organic compounds and understates mass.
A balance reading to at least 0.1 gram, plus tape measure, marker pegs and a random number generator for unbiased plot placement.
Where grazers are present, wire mesh exclosure cages about one metre square.
steps: Confirm the study area is reasonably uniform in vegetation, soil and management; treat clearly different patches as separate strata.
Place at least ten quadrats at randomly generated coordinates. Never choose spots by eye - people unconsciously pick representative-looking or convenient patches.
Clip all herbaceous material rooted inside the frame at ground level. Include plants rooted inside but leaning out; exclude those rooted outside leaning in. Apply the rule consistently.
Bag each quadrat separately, labelled in pencil with site, date and quadrat number.
Sort into current live growth, standing dead from previous seasons, and litter. Exclude standing dead from a current-year estimate.
Dry to constant mass at 60 to 70 degrees Celsius, typically 48 hours. Confirm by reweighing after a further 12 hours rather than assuming.
Weigh each dried sample, divide by quadrat area, then average across quadrats and calculate the standard error so uncertainty is reported rather than hidden.
Repeat every two to three weeks through the season using fresh random quadrats, and take the seasonal maximum.
Where grazing occurs, harvest inside and outside exclosure cages on each date, moving the cages to fresh ground each time so caged vegetation never diverges far from the grazed sward.

sections.heading: Human appropriation of primary production
sections.body:
One of the most striking ways to quantify humanity's ecological footprint is to ask what share of the planet's net primary production people take for themselves. The metric is called HANPP, human appropriation of net primary production, and it was pioneered in a 1986 paper by Peter Vitousek, Paul Ehrlich, Anne Ehrlich and Pamela Matson that remains one of the most cited in ecology.

The accounting has two components. Harvest is the production directly removed - crops, grazed forage, timber, fuelwood, fish - together with the associated material destroyed or left in the field. Land-use change is subtler and larger than people expect: it is the difference between the production a landscape would have generated under its natural vegetation and what it generates now. Converting forest to cropland typically reduces NPP, so the shortfall counts as appropriated even though nobody consumed it. Paving land removes production entirely.

Estimates vary with method and definition, which is worth stating plainly because the headline figures circulate without their caveats. Vitousek's original paper gave a range from about 3 per cent for the narrowest definition, counting only what humans directly eat, to roughly 40 per cent for the broadest, which included forgone production from land-use change and human-caused degradation. Later work by Helmut Haberl and colleagues, using more consistent global data for the year 2000, arrived at approximately 24 per cent of potential terrestrial NPP, comprising around 53 per cent from harvest and the remainder from land-use change. Regional figures are far higher: over 60 per cent in South Asia and much of Europe, under 10 per cent in the Amazon and boreal Siberia.

The significance of these numbers is that they set an upper bound on expansion. If a quarter of terrestrial production is already appropriated, doubling agricultural output cannot come from appropriating another quarter without catastrophic loss of everything else the biosphere does, since the remaining production is what supports all other species and all ecosystem function. This reframes food security away from the amount of land available and toward how efficiently existing production is used - which is why food waste, at roughly a third of production, and the trophic cost of animal agriculture dominate the arithmetic.

Two honest caveats belong with the metric. It measures mass and energy, not value or function, so it treats a hectare of intensively fertilised maize and a hectare of species-rich meadow as comparable if their carbon flows match, which is ecologically obtuse. And the counterfactual natural vegetation is a modelled construct, not an observation, so the land-use-change component inherits all the uncertainty of those models. HANPP is best used as a scale-setting indicator, not a precise ledger.

sections.heading: Too much production: eutrophication and dead zones
sections.body:
Productivity is usually treated as a good thing, and in most contexts it is. But primary production that is not matched by consumption or export becomes a disposal problem, and the result is one of the most widespread forms of aquatic degradation on Earth.

Eutrophication begins with nutrient enrichment, overwhelmingly from agricultural fertiliser runoff, sewage and animal waste, with atmospheric nitrogen deposition contributing in industrialised regions. The immediate response is exactly what you would predict: production rises, sometimes tenfold, and algal biomass accumulates. The damage comes from what happens next. The bloom is not fully grazed - cyanobacteria in particular are poor food and often toxic - so much of it sinks. Bacteria decompose the sinking material, consuming oxygen as they do. In a stratified water body the deep layer is cut off from atmospheric resupply, so oxygen falls. Below about 2 milligrams per litre, conditions are classed as hypoxic and mobile animals flee while sessile ones die. Below roughly 0.5 milligrams per litre, anoxia sets in and sulphate-reducing bacteria begin producing hydrogen sulphide, which is toxic to nearly everything.

The northern Gulf of Mexico dead zone is the best-documented example. Nutrients from the Mississippi basin, draining 41 per cent of the contiguous United States, produce a summer hypoxic area that has typically ranged from about 15,000 to 22,000 square kilometres, with a record near 22,700 square kilometres in 2017. It forms each spring as freshwater discharge stratifies the shelf and breaks up in autumn when storms mix the water column. Similar zones exist in the Baltic Sea, where the problem is chronic and partly self-sustaining because anoxic sediments release stored phosphorus, in the Chesapeake Bay, and in over 400 coastal systems worldwide.

Which nutrient to control is a genuine and long-running scientific dispute rather than a settled matter. Freshwater systems are usually phosphorus-limited, a conclusion established decisively by David Schindler's whole-lake experiments at Canada's Experimental Lakes Area in the 1970s, where a lake divided by a curtain and fertilised differently on each side produced a bloom only on the phosphorus-treated side. Marine systems are more often nitrogen-limited. Estuaries shift seasonally between the two. Because some cyanobacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen and so cannot be starved of it, many limnologists argue phosphorus control is the only reliable lever in fresh water, while others maintain dual control is necessary in transitional waters.

Recovery is slower and less certain than the damage. Lake Erie's phosphorus controls in the 1970s produced genuine improvement within about a decade, then blooms returned in the 2000s driven by dissolved phosphorus from agricultural fields and by invasive mussels altering nutrient cycling. Legacy phosphorus stored in soils and sediments can sustain enrichment for decades after inputs stop, which is the single most important reason to be cautious about promising quick recovery.

sections.heading: Climate change and the future of production
sections.body:
How primary production responds to a changing climate is one of the most consequential open questions in earth system science, because the answer determines how much of humanity's carbon emissions the biosphere will keep absorbing. Land and ocean together currently take up roughly half of annual anthropogenic carbon dioxide emissions, and if that fraction falls, atmospheric concentrations rise faster for the same emissions.

Several forces push in different directions. Carbon dioxide fertilisation is real and measurable: higher concentrations increase photosynthesis in C3 plants and reduce photorespiration, and satellite records show substantial greening of the land surface since the early 1980s, with roughly a quarter to a half of vegetated land showing significant increases in leaf area. Free-air carbon dioxide enrichment experiments, which fumigate intact ecosystems in the field rather than plants in chambers, generally find biomass increases of 10 to 20 per cent for a rise to around 550 parts per million - real, but smaller than early chamber studies suggested, because nutrient limitation quickly reasserts itself. This progressive nitrogen limitation is the key caveat: extra carbon does little if there is no nitrogen or phosphorus with which to build protein.

Warming has mixed effects. It extends growing seasons at high latitudes, which has measurably increased boreal and arctic production. It increases respiration too, and because respiration is typically more temperature-sensitive than photosynthesis, warming can reduce net production even where gross production rises. Above species-specific optima, photosynthesis itself declines. Drought and heatwaves can turn a regional sink into a source within a single season, as European forests did during the 2003 and 2018 events.

The ocean picture is more consistently negative. Warming increases stratification, which reduces the upward mixing of nutrients into the sunlit layer, and most earth system models project a decline in global marine NPP of a few per cent to around 10 per cent by 2100 under high-emission scenarios, with much larger regional changes. Observational confirmation is genuinely difficult because the satellite record is short relative to natural variability and because different algorithms disagree, so this should be described as a robust model expectation with weak observational constraint rather than an established trend.

The honest summary is that the direction of the global response is uncertain and the models disagree substantially. Terrestrial carbon uptake is the single largest source of spread among climate model projections of future atmospheric carbon dioxide. What is reasonably well established is that the current land and ocean sinks are a service the biosphere provides without charge, that this service is not guaranteed to continue at present strength, and that a weakening of it would require deeper emissions cuts to reach the same climate outcome.

sections.heading: Productivity, carbon storage and why the two get confused
sections.body:
A persistent source of muddled thinking, in public debate and sometimes in policy, is the conflation of high productivity with high carbon storage. They are related but distinct, and the distinction decides whether a proposed climate intervention actually works.

Productivity is a flux, the rate of fixation. Storage is a stock, the amount of carbon held. A young fast-growing plantation has high NPP and low storage. An old-growth forest has lower NPP - respiration rises as woody biomass accumulates and growth slows - but very high storage. A peat bog has low productivity by almost any standard, yet northern peatlands hold roughly 500 gigatonnes of carbon, comparable to all the carbon in the atmosphere, because waterlogged anoxic conditions nearly stop decomposition. What accumulates carbon is not fast fixation but slow decomposition.

This is why the intuitive climate solution of planting fast-growing trees is more complicated than it sounds. Rapid growth stores carbon quickly at first, but the carbon is held only as long as the tree stands. Harvest it for paper or fuel and most returns to the atmosphere within years. Timber in buildings holds carbon for decades to a century. The relevant quantity is the product of the storage rate and the residence time, and residence time is usually the neglected term.

Several practical conclusions follow that are worth stating plainly. Protecting existing high-carbon ecosystems is more reliable than creating new ones, because the carbon is already there and avoided loss is immediate while new growth takes decades. Draining a peatland to plant trees, which was done at scale in parts of northern Europe and southeast Asia, is very likely a net carbon source for a long time, because oxidising centuries of peat releases far more than the trees fix. Afforestation at high latitudes carries a further complication: dark conifer canopy over what was snow-covered ground lowers surface albedo enough that the warming from absorbed sunlight can partly or wholly offset the cooling from carbon uptake, a genuinely contested area where the sign of the net effect depends on location and snow duration.

Soil deserves emphasis because it is invisible and enormous. Global soils hold roughly 1,500 to 2,400 gigatonnes of carbon in the top metre, considerably more than vegetation and atmosphere combined. Soil carbon accumulates when inputs from root turnover, exudates and litter exceed microbial decomposition, and it is lost rapidly when tillage exposes protected organic matter to oxygen. Conversion of grassland and forest to cropland has typically released 30 to 50 per cent of original topsoil carbon. Recovering even part of that through reduced tillage, cover cropping and residue retention is real but slow, saturating over decades, and reversible the moment the practice stops.

sections.heading: Common errors, limits and what to do when numbers disagree
sections.body:
Anyone working with productivity figures will encounter contradictions, and most of them come from a small set of recurring problems rather than from genuine scientific dispute.

Check the units first, because this accounts for a startling share of apparent disagreements. Values are quoted as grams of carbon, grams of dry matter, or grams of glucose per square metre per year, and the conversions are not trivial: dry matter is roughly 45 to 48 per cent carbon, so a figure in dry matter is about twice the same value in carbon. Areas may be per square metre or per hectare, a factor of 10,000. Time may be per day or per year. Marine figures are often per square metre of sea surface integrated through the water column, and occasionally per cubic metre, which is not comparable. A twofold discrepancy is almost always a units problem.

Check next whether the figure is gross or net, and whether net means NPP or NEP. Eddy covariance towers report net ecosystem exchange, harvest studies report aboveground NPP, satellite products usually report NPP or GPP depending on the algorithm, and these are not interchangeable. A great many published comparisons quietly compare different quantities.

Ask what was excluded. Belowground production is omitted far more often than stated, and it is 30 to 70 per cent of the total in grassland and perhaps 20 to 40 per cent in forest. Fine root turnover, which can cycle several times a year, is missed by almost every method. Volatile organic compound emission, root exudation to mycorrhizal fungi - which can be 10 to 20 per cent of fixed carbon - and herbivory losses are routinely unmeasured. Nearly every methodological bias runs in the same direction, so published NPP figures should generally be regarded as lower bounds.

Be sceptical of precision. Global NPP is often quoted to three significant figures when the honest uncertainty is 20 to 30 per cent. Regional and biome figures can be worse. Any single number for a biome conceals enormous variation - tropical forest NPP varies more than twofold between sites - and averages across such variation are of limited use for anything local.

Finally, resist the temptation to treat productivity as a proxy for ecological value. A eutrophic lake choked with cyanobacteria can have higher productivity than the clear oligotrophic lake it replaced, and be far worse by every other measure. A monoculture plantation may outproduce the diverse woodland it displaced. Productivity measures the rate of energy capture and nothing else - not biodiversity, not stability, not resilience, not habitat quality, not carbon storage. It is the foundation on which those properties rest, which is precisely why it is worth measuring carefully, but it is not a substitute for measuring them.

guides.title: Biomass and Ecological Production
guides.summary: How living matter accumulates and how fast ecosystems make it: primary and secondary production, the limits that set the rate, how both are measured, and what humans take from the total.

sections.heading: Stock and flow: the distinction everything else rests on
sections.body:
Two quantities describe living matter in an ecosystem, and confusing them is the single most common source of error in the subject. Biomass is a stock: the mass of living material present at one moment, the standing crop, measured in units of mass per unit area such as kilograms per square metre or tonnes per hectare. Production is a flow: the rate at which new living material is made, measured in mass per unit area per unit time, such as grams of carbon per square metre per year. A bank account offers the right analogy. Biomass is the balance; production is the income. Neither can be inferred from the other without knowing something more.

The reason this matters is that stock and flow are frequently uncoupled, sometimes spectacularly. A mature temperate forest carries an enormous standing biomass, perhaps 20 to 40 kilograms of dry matter per square metre, but adds only around 0.5 to 1.5 kilograms per square metre each year, because most of its mass is wood that is structural rather than metabolically active. The open ocean carries a phytoplankton biomass of only about 1 to 10 grams of carbon per square metre, a thousandth of the forest's, yet produces roughly 50 to 150 grams of carbon per square metre per year, because those cells divide and are eaten within days. Turnover time, defined as biomass divided by production, is the quantity that reconciles them: decades to centuries in a forest, days in the plankton.

This uncoupling has consequences for anyone who wants to take something out of an ecosystem. Harvesting is sustainable only when it stays within production, not within biomass. A fishery can remove a large fraction of a fast-turnover stock each year and be replenished; a slow-growing forest or a deep-sea fish population that matures at forty years cannot. Orange roughy, exploited from the 1970s, was fished as though its large standing biomass represented an annual income when in fact it represented a century of accumulated capital, and the stocks collapsed within a decade or two.

The same distinction runs through every application of the subject: through carbon accounting, where biomass is a store and production is a flux; through agriculture, where yield is production of the harvested organ rather than of the whole plant; through bioenergy, where the resource base is annual production and not the standing stock of a forest. When any statement about biomass seems to conflict with a statement about productivity, the resolution is nearly always that one is describing the balance and the other the income. A useful habit is to check the units before anything else: if the quantity has time in its denominator it is a rate and belongs to production, and if it does not it is a stock and belongs to biomass. Phrases such as 'the productivity of the forest is 300 tonnes per hectare' are self-evidently confused, and the confusion is common enough in popular writing that the check is worth applying every time.

sections.heading: Units, conversions and how the accounting is kept
sections.body:
Living tissue is mostly water, and water content varies enormously between a succulent leaf and a piece of heartwood, so fresh mass is nearly useless for comparison. The convention is therefore dry mass, obtained by drying a sample to constant weight at 60 to 105 degrees Celsius. Sixty is preferred where volatile compounds matter and 105 where only water is being driven off. Even dry mass is imperfect, because a gram of lignin-rich wood and a gram of protein-rich leaf are not equivalent chemically, so ecologists working across systems usually convert to carbon or to energy.

The carbon convention is that dry plant biomass is approximately 47 to 50 per cent carbon by mass, so a factor of 0.475 to 0.50 converts dry mass to carbon mass. Wood tends toward the upper end and leaves and fine roots slightly lower. Ash content, the mineral residue after combustion, is typically 1 to 3 per cent in wood, 5 to 10 per cent in herbaceous foliage and can exceed 20 per cent in some algae and grasses, which is why ash-free dry mass is specified in aquatic work. Energy content is remarkably consistent for plant material at roughly 17 to 20 megajoules per kilogram of dry mass, rising to 20 to 24 for animal tissue because fat carries about 39 megajoules per kilogram against 17 for carbohydrate.

For aquatic systems, biomass is often expressed as chlorophyll-a concentration in milligrams per cubic metre, because chlorophyll is easy to measure by fluorescence and by satellite. Converting it to carbon requires a carbon-to-chlorophyll ratio that is not constant: it ranges from about 20 in low light and nutrient-rich water to 200 or more in bright, nutrient-poor surface water, because cells build more pigment when light is scarce. Any global carbon figure derived from satellite chlorophyll therefore carries this ratio as a substantial and often unstated uncertainty.

At the global scale the numbers are large enough to need their own unit, the petagram, equal to 10 to the power 15 grams, one billion tonnes, and identical to the gigatonne. The current best estimates, from the biomass census of Bar-On, Phillips and Milo published in 2018, put total living biomass on Earth at roughly 550 petagrams of carbon, of which plants are about 450, bacteria about 70, fungi about 12, archaea about 7, animals about 2, and humans about 0.06. Livestock outweigh all wild mammals by roughly an order of magnitude, and the biomass of domesticated poultry exceeds that of all wild birds. These figures carry uncertainties of tens of per cent, particularly for soil microbes and deep-subsurface life, but the orders of magnitude are robust and they reframe most intuitions about what the biosphere is mostly made of.

sections.heading: The engine: photosynthesis and the capture of sunlight
sections.body:
Essentially all ecological production begins with photosynthesis, the reduction of carbon dioxide to carbohydrate using energy captured from light. The overall reaction takes six molecules of carbon dioxide and six of water to one of glucose and six of oxygen, requiring about 2,870 kilojoules per mole of glucose formed. The reaction proceeds in two connected stages. In the light reactions, held in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts, photons excite electrons in chlorophyll, which are passed down a transport chain that pumps protons across the membrane and ultimately reduces the carrier NADP to NADPH, while the proton gradient drives the synthesis of ATP. Water is split to replace the lost electrons, and the oxygen we breathe is the discarded by-product of that split.

In the second stage, the Calvin-Benson cycle, the enzyme ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase, universally shortened to Rubisco, attaches carbon dioxide to a five-carbon sugar. Rubisco is almost certainly the most abundant protein on Earth, and it is strikingly inefficient: it processes only a few molecules per second, and it confuses oxygen with carbon dioxide, initiating a wasteful pathway called photorespiration that can consume 20 to 30 per cent of the carbon fixed in warm conditions. This single enzymatic flaw, an inheritance from an atmosphere that once had almost no oxygen, sets an upper bound on the productivity of most plants.

Two workarounds evolved repeatedly. C4 photosynthesis, found in maize, sugarcane, sorghum and most tropical grasses, first fixes carbon into a four-carbon acid in outer cells and then pumps it into internal bundle-sheath cells where Rubisco operates in a carbon-dioxide-enriched compartment, suppressing photorespiration. It costs extra ATP but pays handsomely above about 25 degrees Celsius, which is why C4 crops hold the record productivities. Crassulacean acid metabolism, found in cacti and many succulents, separates the steps in time rather than space, opening stomata only at night to collect carbon dioxide and processing it by day with the pores shut, saving water at a substantial cost in growth rate.

The efficiency of the whole process is low, and knowing how low is essential to any realistic thinking about bioenergy. Of incoming solar radiation, only about 45 per cent falls in the photosynthetically active waveband of 400 to 700 nanometres. Of that, reflection, transmission and the quantum requirement of the reactions leave a theoretical maximum conversion of roughly 4.6 per cent for C3 plants and 6 per cent for C4. Respiration removes a third to a half again. Real field crops achieve 1 to 2 per cent over a growing season, and whole natural ecosystems average around 0.3 per cent. Photovoltaic panels convert 15 to 22 per cent, which is why land-area comparisons between the two are so lopsided.

sections.heading: Gross, net and everything that leaks in between
sections.body:
Production is measured at several nested levels, and quoting the wrong one is a frequent source of apparent disagreement between studies. Gross primary production is the total carbon fixed by photosynthesis before the plant spends any of it. Globally it runs at approximately 120 to 130 petagrams of carbon per year, split fairly evenly between land and ocean. Plants immediately respire a large fraction of this to power their own maintenance and growth, an expenditure called autotrophic respiration, which consumes roughly half of gross production in most ecosystems and rather more in warm, structurally complex forests where there is a great deal of living tissue to maintain.

What survives is net primary production, the carbon actually available to build plant tissue and, by extension, to feed everything else. Global net primary production is about 105 to 115 petagrams of carbon per year, of which land contributes roughly 56 to 60 and the ocean roughly 48 to 54. That near-parity is remarkable given that the ocean holds under one per cent of the planet's photosynthetic biomass, and it is entirely a consequence of turnover: marine phytoplankton replace their entire biomass every two to six days, whereas terrestrial vegetation takes years to decades.

Subtracting the respiration of everything that is not a plant gives net ecosystem production. Heterotrophic respiration comes from herbivores, predators and, overwhelmingly, from decomposers processing dead material in soil and sediment. In a mature ecosystem at equilibrium, net ecosystem production is close to zero, because decomposition has caught up with production. Positive values mean the system is accumulating carbon, as in a regrowing forest; negative values mean it is losing carbon, as in a drained peatland where decomposition of ancient stored material outruns present-day photosynthesis. A final level, net biome production, subtracts losses to fire, harvest, erosion and export by rivers, and is the quantity that actually matters for the atmosphere at large scales.

Two further subtleties routinely trip people up. First, a substantial share of net primary production is never seen as visible plant tissue at all: 10 to 30 per cent may be released underground as root exudates or transferred directly to mycorrhizal fungi, and methods based only on harvesting shoots miss all of it. Second, a large fraction of what is measured as growth in trees is replacement of fine roots and leaves that live less than a year, so annual production can be several times the annual increase in standing biomass. A forest whose biomass is not changing at all may still be producing one or two kilograms of dry matter per square metre each year, all of which passes straight through to the detrital system.

sections.heading: What sets the rate: light, water, nutrients and heat
sections.body:
Production is limited by whichever requirement is in shortest supply relative to demand, an idea formalised in the nineteenth century as Liebig's law of the minimum after Justus von Liebig, though it was first stated by Carl Sprengel in 1828. The metaphor of a barrel whose capacity is set by its shortest stave captures it well enough for a single limiting factor, but real systems are usually co-limited: adding nitrogen alone may do nothing until phosphorus is also supplied, because the organisms need both in a roughly fixed ratio.

On land, water is the dominant control across the great majority of the surface. Photosynthesis requires open stomata, open stomata lose water, and the exchange rate is brutal: a plant typically loses 200 to 1,000 grams of water for every gram of dry matter it makes, a quantity called transpiration ratio. Annual net primary production therefore correlates strongly with annual precipitation up to around 2,000 to 2,500 millimetres, after which the relationship flattens because light and nutrients take over as the constraint. Temperature matters through the length of the growing season more than through instantaneous rates, which is why boreal forests are unproductive despite ample summer light.

Nutrients set the ceiling wherever water and light are adequate. Nitrogen limits most temperate and boreal systems, because although the atmosphere is 78 per cent nitrogen gas, the triple bond in that molecule requires either lightning, industrial synthesis, or the nitrogenase enzyme of a small number of bacteria to break. Phosphorus limits many tropical soils, which are ancient and deeply weathered so that the rock-derived phosphorus has long since been leached away or locked into iron and aluminium minerals. The distinction has practical consequences: fertilising a temperate grassland with nitrogen produces a response, while doing the same on a weathered tropical soil often does not.

In the ocean, light and nutrients are spatially separated, which is the central problem of marine productivity. Light penetrates only the upper tens of metres, while nutrients accumulate at depth where sinking organic matter decomposes. Production is therefore concentrated wherever the two are brought together: coastal upwelling zones along the eastern boundaries of oceans, where wind-driven offshore transport draws deep water to the surface; regions of seasonal mixing; and the edges of currents. Iron is the limiting nutrient across roughly a third of the ocean, the so-called high-nutrient low-chlorophyll regions of the Southern Ocean and equatorial Pacific, where nitrate is abundant but the dust-borne iron supply is not, a hypothesis proposed by John Martin in the late 1980s and since confirmed by more than a dozen deliberate fertilisation experiments. Those experiments reliably produce a bloom; whether the carbon fixed actually sinks and is stored for centuries, rather than being respired near the surface, is much less certain, and it is the reason ocean iron fertilisation remains a contested proposal rather than an accepted climate tool.

sections.heading: The global pattern: where production actually happens
sections.body:
Net primary production varies by more than two orders of magnitude across the Earth's surface, and the pattern is largely predictable from climate. Tropical rainforests are the most productive terrestrial systems, at roughly 2,000 to 2,500 grams of dry matter per square metre per year, because they combine high light, abundant water and a year-round growing season. Swamps, marshes and estuaries match or exceed them, at 2,000 to 4,000, which is why coastal wetlands punch so far above their area in carbon and fisheries terms. Temperate forests fall around 1,000 to 1,500, boreal forests 500 to 800, temperate grasslands 300 to 800, tundra 100 to 200 and true desert below 100, sometimes below 10.

Because area matters as much as rate, the ranking by total contribution differs from the ranking by intensity. Tropical forests deliver roughly a third of all terrestrial net primary production from about a tenth of the ice-free land surface. Savannas and tropical grasslands, individually unremarkable per square metre, cover so much ground that they contribute a comparable total and dominate the year-to-year variability of the whole land carbon sink, because their production swings with rainfall. Deserts and semi-deserts occupy nearly a third of the land and contribute a few per cent.

In the ocean the pattern is close to inverted relative to intuition. The great subtropical gyres, which occupy about 40 per cent of the ocean surface and look a deep clear blue precisely because there is nothing in them, produce under 50 grams of carbon per square metre per year and are among the least productive habitats on Earth, comparable to desert. Continental shelves and upwelling zones produce 300 to over 1,000. The five major eastern-boundary upwelling systems, off Peru, California, northwest and southwest Africa, cover well under one per cent of the ocean and supply something like a fifth of the world's wild fish catch.

The seasonal dimension is as important as the geographic one. In temperate seas a spring bloom occurs when the water column stratifies enough to keep cells in the light while winter-mixed nutrients are still present, followed by a nutrient-starved summer and often a smaller autumn bloom when storms mix the column again. Sverdrup's critical depth hypothesis of 1953 explained the timing as the point at which the mixed layer becomes shallower than the depth at which integrated photosynthesis balances integrated respiration. The picture has since been complicated by evidence that reduced turbulence, rather than stratification depth alone, can trigger blooms, and the relative importance of the two mechanisms remains an active argument. Polar seas compress the whole annual cycle into a few intense weeks, which is why Antarctic and Arctic food webs are so short and so dependent on precise timing: a bloom that arrives two weeks early relative to the hatching of the animals that graze it can propagate a failure all the way up to seabirds and whales in the same season.

sections.heading: Secondary production and the cost of every step up
sections.body:
Secondary production is the generation of new biomass by consumers: herbivores, predators, parasites and decomposers, all of which build their tissue from organic matter someone else made. Every transfer is lossy, and understanding where the losses go explains most of the structure of food webs. Of the energy available at one level, some is never eaten at all, some is eaten but not digested and leaves as faeces, some is digested but respired to power movement and maintenance, and only the remainder becomes new consumer tissue.

These stages are separated by named efficiencies. Consumption efficiency is the fraction of available production actually ingested, ranging from under 5 per cent for herbivores eating forest wood to 50 or even 90 per cent for zooplankton grazing phytoplankton, which is why the ocean can support so much animal life on so little standing plant biomass. Assimilation efficiency, the fraction of ingested energy absorbed across the gut, is 20 to 50 per cent for herbivores chewing cellulose that vertebrates cannot digest without microbial help, and 60 to 90 per cent for carnivores eating tissue chemically similar to their own. Production efficiency, the fraction of assimilated energy converted to new tissue rather than respired, is where the deepest split lies: 30 to 40 per cent in insects and other invertebrates, 5 to 10 per cent in fish and other ectothermic vertebrates, and 1 to 3 per cent in birds and mammals, which spend the overwhelming majority of their intake keeping warm.

Multiplying the three gives trophic transfer efficiency, the fraction of one level's production that becomes the next level's production. The textbook figure of 10 per cent, popularised by Raymond Lindeman's foundational 1942 paper on trophic dynamics in Cedar Bog Lake, is a reasonable central estimate but conceals wide variation: marine planktonic systems often achieve 10 to 20 per cent, while terrestrial systems built on woody plants and endothermic consumers may manage 1 to 5 per cent.

The arithmetic explains why food chains are short. Starting from 1,000 units of plant production and losing 90 per cent per step leaves 100 for herbivores, 10 for primary carnivores, 1 for secondary carnivores and 0.1 for the next. Beyond four or five levels there is simply not enough energy to support a viable population of animals large enough to eat the level below. It also explains why top predators are rare, why they need vast territories, why they are so vulnerable to habitat fragmentation, and why eating plants directly feeds far more people per hectare than eating animals that ate the plants: the conversion ratio for beef is roughly 25 kilograms of feed per kilogram of edible protein, against about 2 to 3 for chicken and near 1 for a directly eaten grain.

sections.heading: Pyramids, and the ones that stand on their heads
sections.body:
Charles Elton introduced the pyramid diagram in 1927 as a way of showing how ecosystems thin out toward the top, and three versions are in use. A pyramid of numbers counts individuals at each level. A pyramid of biomass shows the standing mass. A pyramid of energy shows the production flowing through each level per unit time. They are not interchangeable, and the differences between them are informative rather than inconvenient.

Pyramids of numbers invert easily and trivially. A single mature oak supports thousands of caterpillars, so the herbivore level outnumbers the producer level by orders of magnitude; add the parasitoid wasps inside the caterpillars and the diagram inverts again. Nothing deep is happening here, only that individuals differ in size by a factor of a billion, which is exactly why counting individuals is a poor way to characterise a food web.

Pyramids of biomass invert for a more interesting reason. In open-ocean plankton communities, the standing biomass of zooplankton frequently exceeds that of the phytoplankton they eat. This looks impossible until turnover is taken into account: the phytoplankton are replaced every few days while the copepods grazing them live for weeks, so a small but furiously replenished producer stock supports a larger but slower consumer stock. The measured biomass is a snapshot of a stock, and stocks say nothing about the flow through them. The same effect appears on healthy coral reefs, where surveys around remote unfished Pacific atolls have found predator biomass exceeding prey biomass, sustained by the rapid turnover of small prey fish.

The pyramid of energy, by contrast, can never invert. Because each transfer loses energy irreversibly to respiration and heat, and because the second law of thermodynamics does not negotiate, the production flowing through a level is always less than the production flowing through the level below it. This makes the energy pyramid the only one that is guaranteed to be shaped like a pyramid and the only one whose shape carries a hard physical meaning. When a diagram in a textbook shows an inverted biomass pyramid as though it were a paradox, the resolution is always the same: draw the energy version instead, and it will stand the right way up. The general lesson generalises beyond ecology, since it is the same distinction between reservoir and flux that governs water in a catchment or money in an economy.

One further complication makes real food webs messier than any pyramid suggests. Trophic levels are an abstraction, and most animals do not occupy one. An omnivorous fish that eats algae as a juvenile, invertebrates as a sub-adult and other fish when large moves up the web as it grows, and a great many species feed at two or three levels simultaneously. Ecologists therefore increasingly report a continuous trophic position, often estimated from the ratio of nitrogen-15 to nitrogen-14 in tissue, which rises by roughly 3.4 parts per thousand with each transfer. A value of 3.7 means an animal is feeding somewhere between the second and third levels, which is a more honest description of most predators than assigning them to a tier.

sections.heading: The detrital pathway: where most production actually goes
sections.body:
The grazing food chain that runs plant to herbivore to carnivore is the version usually drawn, and in most ecosystems it is the minority pathway. Between 50 and 90 per cent of terrestrial net primary production is never eaten alive at all; it dies as leaf litter, fallen wood, root turnover and root exudate, and enters the detrital food web. In forests the figure is at the top of that range. Only in grazing-dominated systems such as grasslands and the plankton does the living pathway carry a comparable share, and even there the faeces of the grazers rejoin the detrital pool almost immediately.

Decomposition proceeds through physical fragmentation by soil invertebrates such as earthworms, mites and springtails, followed by enzymatic breakdown by fungi and bacteria. Rate depends on temperature, moisture, oxygen availability and the chemistry of the litter, summarised for practical purposes by the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio and the lignin content. Litter with a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio below about 25 decomposes rapidly and releases mineral nitrogen; above about 30, decomposers must scavenge nitrogen from the surrounding soil to build their own tissue, immobilising it and slowing plant growth. This is the mechanism behind the familiar gardening warning that digging in fresh sawdust or straw temporarily starves a bed of nitrogen.

Where decomposition cannot keep up with production, carbon accumulates. Waterlogging is the commonest cause, because oxygen diffuses about ten thousand times more slowly through water than air, so saturated soils go anaerobic and decomposition slows by an order of magnitude.
