Peatlands cover roughly 3 per cent of the land surface yet hold something like 500 to 600 petagrams of carbon, comparable to all the carbon in the atmosphere and about twice that in the world's forest biomass. Cold has the same effect through temperature alone, which is why permafrost soils store a further 1,000 to 1,600 petagrams.

Soil as a whole holds two to three times more carbon than living vegetation, and the residence time of that carbon spans an enormous range: fresh litter turns over in months, particulate organic matter in years to decades, and mineral-associated organic matter that is physically protected inside soil aggregates or bound to clay surfaces persists for centuries to millennia. The older view that this persistence came from the intrinsic chemical recalcitrance of humic substances has largely been abandoned since around 2011 in favour of a view emphasising physical protection and microbial access, a genuine and fairly recent shift in the field that older textbooks do not reflect.

The practical importance of the detrital route is that it decouples an ecosystem's carbon balance from its productivity. A forest can be highly productive and still lose carbon overall if warming or drainage accelerates decomposition faster than it accelerates growth, and an unproductive bog can be a powerful net sink because almost nothing decomposes. Any scheme that proposes to store carbon in land therefore has to make a claim about the decomposition side of the ledger, not only about how much is grown, and claims that quantify only the growth are incomplete by construction.

sections.heading: Measuring biomass and production on land
sections.body:
The oldest and most direct method is harvest. Everything within a defined quadrat is cut, sorted, dried and weighed, and for annual herbaceous vegetation the peak standing crop is a fair approximation of annual net primary production because the whole year's growth is present at once. The method is destructive, laborious and systematically biased low, because it misses everything that died and decomposed earlier in the season, everything eaten by herbivores, and everything below ground. In grasslands, correcting for turnover typically raises the estimate by 20 to 50 per cent, and including roots can double it, since many grasslands allocate more than half their production below ground.

For forests, harvesting is obviously impractical, so biomass is estimated from allometry: statistical relationships that predict whole-tree mass from easily measured dimensions. Diameter at breast height, measured at 1.3 metres, is the usual predictor, and equations take the form of mass equal to a coefficient multiplied by diameter raised to a power near 2.4, sometimes with height and wood density as additional terms. Pantropical equations published by Jérôme Chave and colleagues in 2005 and revised in 2014 are widely used. Applying an equation outside the size range or forest type it was fitted on is the commonest error, and extrapolating to very large trees is particularly dangerous because they are rare in the calibration data yet carry a disproportionate share of the biomass.

Production in forests is measured as the annual increment: repeated diameter measurements, usually with permanent dendrometer bands, plus litterfall collected in traps, plus an estimate of fine-root turnover from soil cores or minirhizotrons. Fine roots are the weakest link and are often the largest single uncertainty in a forest carbon budget.
steps: Define the sampling design first: locate plots randomly or on a systematic grid, sized to the vegetation, roughly 0.25 to 1 square metre for grassland and 20 by 20 metres or larger for forest.
For herbaceous vegetation, clip all live material to ground level at peak standing crop, separating live from dead and by species if the question requires it.
Extract root biomass with cores of known volume, wash over a 0.5 millimetre sieve, and separate live from dead roots by colour, texture and buoyancy, accepting that this step is subjective.
Dry every sample to constant mass at 65 degrees Celsius, usually 48 to 72 hours, and weigh on a balance reading to 0.01 gram; record the mass at two time points to confirm it has stopped falling.
For forests, record diameter at breast height for every stem above the threshold, with species and, on a subsample, height, and re-measure the same tagged stems annually.
Choose an allometric equation matched to the forest type, size range and wood density of your site, and report which one you used, since equation choice can change the answer by 20 per cent or more.
Collect litterfall in traps of known area emptied monthly, dry and weigh, and add the annual total to the stem increment.
Convert dry mass to carbon using a measured factor where possible, and propagate the uncertainty of every step rather than reporting a single figure.

sections.heading: Measuring production in water
sections.body:
Aquatic production cannot be harvested, because the producers are microscopic, drifting and replaced within days. The classic approach instead measures the metabolic signature of photosynthesis in a confined sample. In the light-and-dark bottle method, water is sealed into paired transparent and opaque bottles and suspended at the depth it came from for a few hours. In the light bottle, photosynthesis and respiration both occur, so the oxygen change gives net production. In the dark bottle only respiration occurs, so the oxygen decline gives community respiration. Adding the two gives gross production. The oxygen is measured by Winkler titration, a chemical method dating from 1888 that remains the reference standard, or increasingly by optical sensors.

For the open ocean this method is too insensitive, because production is low and the oxygen change over a few hours is smaller than the measurement error. The alternative, introduced by Einer Steemann Nielsen in 1952, adds a trace of radioactive carbon-14 as bicarbonate, incubates, filters the cells and counts the radioactivity they have taken up. It is far more sensitive but its interpretation is genuinely ambiguous: short incubations of two to four hours approximate gross production while incubations of a full day approach net production, because respiration progressively releases the labelled carbon. Much of the historical literature is not explicit about which it reports.

Both bottle methods share a serious limitation known as the bottle effect. Enclosing water excludes turbulence, concentrates or removes grazers, allows bacteria to grow on the container walls and can contaminate the sample with trace metals, all of which change the result within hours. Modern work therefore increasingly relies on unconfined tracer approaches such as the natural oxygen-18 isotope ratio, the triple-oxygen-isotope method, and free-water diel oxygen budgets, in which a moored sensor records the daily oxygen cycle of the whole water body and production is inferred from it.
ingredients: Paired biological oxygen demand bottles, typically 300 millilitres, in clear glass and in opaque or foil-wrapped form, plus a third for the initial measurement.
A Niskin or Van Dorn water sampler that closes at a chosen depth, so the sample comes from the light environment being studied.
Winkler reagents: manganous sulphate solution, alkaline potassium iodide with sodium azide, concentrated sulphuric acid, standardised sodium thiosulphate titrant and a starch indicator.
A burette reading to 0.02 millilitres, or a calibrated optical dissolved-oxygen probe as a faster alternative.
A mooring line, clips and a float, so the bottles can be returned to their original depth for the incubation.
A filtration rig with glass-fibre filters, a fluorometer or spectrophotometer and acetone, for the paired chlorophyll-a measurement that lets production be normalised to biomass.
A submersible light meter or photosynthetically active radiation sensor, so the depth of each incubation can be expressed as a fraction of surface light rather than merely in metres.
Acid-washed glassware and powder-free gloves throughout, since trace-metal contamination from bare hands or ordinary detergent can suppress production in oligotrophic seawater by a measurable amount.

sections.heading: Seeing production from orbit, and modelling what cannot be seen
sections.body:
Field measurements cover an infinitesimal fraction of the Earth, so global estimates of production come from satellites. The underlying physics is simple: chlorophyll absorbs strongly in the red, around 660 nanometres, while leaf internal structure scatters near-infrared light strongly, around 850 nanometres. The contrast between the two bands is captured by the normalised difference vegetation index, the difference divided by the sum, which runs near zero for bare soil, above 0.6 for dense green canopy and negative over water. It has been computed continuously since the launch of Landsat in 1972 and the AVHRR sensors from 1978, giving a record long enough to detect trends.

Turning an index into a production figure uses the light-use efficiency framework proposed by John Monteith in 1972: production equals incoming photosynthetically active radiation, multiplied by the fraction the canopy absorbs, multiplied by an efficiency with which absorbed light is converted to biomass. The absorbed fraction is estimated from the vegetation index; the efficiency is assigned by vegetation type, typically 0.3 to 1.5 grams of carbon per megajoule, and then reduced by scalars for temperature and water stress. The operational MODIS product built on this logic has produced global eight-day maps since 2000.

The independent check on all of this comes from eddy covariance, a micrometeorological technique in which a sonic anemometer and a fast gas analyser mounted on a tower measure vertical wind speed and carbon dioxide concentration ten to twenty times a second. Multiplying the fluctuations together and averaging gives the net vertical flux of carbon dioxide directly, integrated over a footprint of hundreds of metres upwind. The FLUXNET network of several hundred such towers, running since the 1990s, is the backbone of validation. Its own limitations are real: the technique underestimates flux on calm nights when turbulence dies and the air drains downhill, requiring a friction-velocity filter and gap filling that introduce their own assumptions.

In the ocean the equivalent chain runs from ocean-colour sensors, beginning with the Coastal Zone Colour Scanner in 1978 and continuing through SeaWiFS and MODIS, to chlorophyll concentration, to production via models such as the vertically generalised production model of Behrenfeld and Falkowski from 1997. Different published models applied to identical satellite data disagree on global marine production by roughly a factor of two. Satellites also see only the top optical depth, missing the deep chlorophyll maximum that can hold a substantial share of production in stratified tropical waters, which is why autonomous profiling floats carrying optical sensors have become important.

A newer generation of measurements is beginning to bypass the index-and-efficiency chain altogether. Solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence, the faint re-emission of absorbed light at around 740 nanometres that satellites such as GOME-2, OCO-2 and TROPOMI can detect, is emitted by the photosynthetic machinery while it is actually running rather than merely by green tissue that exists. It therefore tracks production more directly, and notably falls during drought stress at a point when a vegetation index still reports a healthy green canopy. The signal is faint and its relationship to carbon uptake is not yet fully pinned down, so it supplements rather than replaces the established products.

sections.heading: The human share: appropriation of primary production
sections.body:
One species now intercepts a large fraction of the planet's terrestrial production. The accounting framework is called the human appropriation of net primary production, and it counts two distinct things: the biomass humans actually harvest, and the production foregone because land has been converted to a less productive use than the vegetation it replaced. A wheat field on land that once carried woodland is counted twice over, once for the grain removed and once for the difference between what the woodland would have produced and what the field does.

Estimates converge on roughly 20 to 30 per cent of potential terrestrial net primary production being appropriated, with the widely cited analysis by Helmut Haberl and colleagues in 2007 putting the figure near 24 per cent for the year 2000. Regional values are far higher: over 60 per cent across much of South Asia and Western Europe, near zero in boreal Siberia and the Amazon interior. Around half the total is harvested biomass, of which the great majority is livestock feed and grazed vegetation rather than food eaten directly, and a further large share is production lost to land conversion, with fire management and infrastructure making up the rest.

The most striking consequence is how the appropriated flow is distributed among species. Because domesticated animals eat an enormous share of the harvested production, the biomass of livestock now exceeds that of all wild terrestrial mammals by roughly a factor of fifteen to twenty. This is the clearest single measure of ecological dominance available, and it is a statement about production capture rather than about hunting or habitat loss considered separately. Wild animal populations are constrained less by direct persecution than by the fact that the energy they would have eaten now flows through cattle, pigs and chickens.

Agricultural yields have risen dramatically without proportionally increasing total plant production, which is a distinction worth being clear about. Cereal yields roughly tripled between 1960 and 2020, driven by nitrogen fertiliser synthesised through the Haber-Bosch process, by irrigation, and by breeding that shifted the harvest index — the proportion of a plant's biomass in the harvested grain — from around 0.3 to 0.5 or above. Semi-dwarf wheat and rice varieties of the Green Revolution did not photosynthesise faster; they put a larger share of what they made into grain and stood up under heavy fertilisation instead of falling over. That particular lever is close to exhausted, since harvest index cannot exceed one and the plant still needs stems and roots, which is why current yield-improvement research targets photosynthesis itself.

How much room remains is a real question rather than a rhetorical one. Roughly a third of harvested crop production is lost or wasted between field and plate, and the conversion losses in feeding grain to animals are, as trophic arithmetic dictates, severe. Both represent appropriated production that never feeds anyone. Whether the humane conclusion is to raise production further or to lose less of what is already made is a question about policy and diet rather than about ecology, but the ecological accounting makes the size of each lever plain.

sections.heading: Bioenergy: turning production into fuel, and what it costs
sections.body:
Biomass was humanity's principal energy source until the nineteenth century and still supplies roughly 9 to 10 per cent of global primary energy, most of it wood, charcoal, dung and crop residues burned for cooking and heating in low-income households, often at serious cost to indoor air quality. Modern bioenergy — pellet-fired power stations, ethanol from maize or sugarcane, biodiesel from oil crops, biogas from anaerobic digestion — is a much smaller share but attracts most of the policy attention because it is dispatchable and, in principle, carbon-neutral.

The physical constraint is the low efficiency with which plants capture sunlight. A high-yielding energy crop such as Miscanthus produces perhaps 15 to 25 tonnes of dry matter per hectare per year in a favourable temperate climate, sugarcane in the tropics 30 to 40 including its residue. At 18 megajoules per kilogram, 20 tonnes per hectare represents 360 gigajoules per hectare per year, which is about 1.1 watts per square metre averaged over the year. Converting that to electricity at 35 per cent efficiency leaves about 0.4 watts per square metre. A photovoltaic installation in the same field delivers 5 to 20 watts per square metre of electricity. The land-area ratio between the two is therefore an order of magnitude or more, and no plausible improvement in crop breeding closes it.

Energy return on investment is the second constraint. Maize ethanol in the United States has an energy return of roughly 1.2 to 1.6 to one once the diesel, fertiliser and distillation energy are counted, which is barely better than break-even; Brazilian sugarcane ethanol achieves 8 to 10 to one because the crop is more productive and the bagasse residue fuels the distillery. Wood chips burned locally for heat can exceed 20 to one. The variation is enormous, and any general claim about bioenergy that does not specify feedstock, location and end use is close to meaningless.

The carbon-neutrality claim requires care and has been the subject of legitimate scientific dispute. Burning biomass releases carbon immediately while regrowing it takes time, so there is a carbon debt period during which atmospheric concentrations are higher than they would have been. For annual crop residues that period is under a year and neutrality is a fair approximation. For whole mature trees harvested for pellets it can be 40 to 100 years, which is the wrong side of the timescales that matter for climate targets. Add indirect land-use change, where displacing food production onto new land releases stored carbon elsewhere, and some biofuel pathways have been shown to be worse than the fossil fuel they replace. The defensible cases are wastes, residues and genuinely marginal land.

sections.heading: Production in a changing climate
sections.body:
Terrestrial production has increased over the satellite era. Multiple independent lines of evidence — vegetation indices, the widening seasonal amplitude of atmospheric carbon dioxide measured at Mauna Loa since 1958, and the land carbon sink inferred from the global budget — indicate a greening trend and a land sink currently absorbing roughly 3 petagrams of carbon per year, about 30 per cent of human emissions. The ocean takes up a further 2.5 to 3 petagrams, mostly by physical dissolution rather than biology. Without these two sinks the atmospheric concentration would be rising roughly twice as fast as it is.

Several mechanisms contribute and their relative weights are contested. Carbon dioxide fertilisation is real: raising concentration increases photosynthesis in C3 plants by suppressing photorespiration, and free-air enrichment experiments running since the 1990s typically show 10 to 25 per cent production gains at 550 parts per million. But the gains are smaller in the field than in chambers, they fade as nitrogen or phosphorus become limiting, and C4 plants respond little because they already concentrate carbon dioxide internally. Longer growing seasons in high latitudes, nitrogen deposition from agriculture and combustion, and the regrowth of previously cleared land all contribute as well, and separating them is genuinely difficult.

The countervailing processes are becoming more visible. Respiration and decomposition increase with temperature faster than photosynthesis does over much of the relevant range, so warming eventually turns a sink into a source. Drought, which is intensifying in many regions, suppresses production sharply: the 2003 European heatwave reduced the continent's gross primary production by around 30 per cent and turned the land from sink to source for that year. Rising vapour-pressure deficit closes stomata even where soil water is adequate. Fire, insect outbreaks and permafrost thaw all release stored carbon, and the permafrost pool is roughly twice the size of the atmospheric one.

The honest position is that the future trajectory of the land sink is one of the largest uncertainties in climate projection. Earth system models disagree not merely on magnitude but on sign by the late twenty-first century, with some projecting continued uptake and others a substantial source. The disagreement traces mainly to how models represent nutrient limitation on carbon dioxide fertilisation and the temperature sensitivity of soil decomposition, both of which are poorly constrained by observation. Anyone presenting a confident single number for how much carbon land ecosystems will absorb in 2080 is going beyond what the evidence supports.

Marine production carries its own set of uncertain trends. Warming increases stratification, which reduces the upward supply of nutrients and is expected to lower open-ocean production in the low latitudes while retreating sea ice raises it near the poles. Estimates of the trend in global marine production over the satellite era vary in sign between analyses, partly because the record is short relative to natural climate oscillations such as the El Nino cycle, which swings equatorial Pacific production by tens of per cent from year to year and can masquerade as a trend in a two-decade series.

sections.heading: When production goes wrong, and what can be done
sections.body:
Too little production and too much are both failure modes. Excess is the more counterintuitive. Loading a water body with nitrogen and phosphorus from fertiliser runoff, sewage or detergent removes the nutrient limit and production explodes, a process called eutrophication. The algae are not the problem; their decomposition is. When the bloom dies and sinks, decomposers consume oxygen faster than it can be resupplied through a stratified water column, and the bottom water goes hypoxic below about 2 milligrams of oxygen per litre, at which point fish flee and immobile animals die. The Gulf of Mexico dead zone driven by the Mississippi basin reaches 15,000 to 22,000 square kilometres most summers, and more than 700 coastal systems worldwide now report the condition.

Recovery is possible but slow and asymmetric, because phosphorus accumulated in sediments continues to release for years after inputs stop, a phenomenon called internal loading. Lake Erie improved substantially after phosphorus controls in the 1970s and then deteriorated again from the mid-1990s as dissolved-phosphorus runoff patterns changed, which is a useful caution against assuming that a fixed problem stays fixed. The general lesson is that reducing inputs is necessary but the lag between action and response is measured in years to decades.

Depleted production is the more familiar failure. Overgrazing, over-cultivation, salinisation from irrigation and soil erosion all reduce the rate at which land can make biomass, and the degradation is self-reinforcing because lower plant cover means less organic matter, poorer water retention and more erosion. Reversal is possible and comparatively well understood: restoring plant cover, adding organic matter, reducing tillage, and matching stocking rates to actual forage production rather than to habit. Where soil carbon has been depleted by decades of cultivation there is real scope for rebuilding it, though claims about the magnitude and permanence of agricultural soil carbon sequestration are frequently overstated, and the gains saturate after two to three decades as the soil approaches a new equilibrium.

The single most useful discipline in all of this is the one that opens the subject: distinguish the stock from the flow, and set any extraction against the flow. A fishery managed to maximum sustainable yield targets the surplus production of the stock, which peaks not at maximum biomass but at roughly 30 to 50 per cent of unfished biomass, because that is where per-capita growth and total numbers are jointly greatest. A woodlot managed on rotation takes an annual increment. A grazing system stocked to the production of a bad year rather than an average one survives droughts. In each case the mistake that destroys the resource is the same: treating an accumulated stock as though it were annual income, and discovering only afterwards how long the accumulation took.

guides.title: Nuclear Power: How a Reactor Makes Electricity, Uranium Fuel, Radiation, Waste and Cost
guides.summary: Nuclear energy from the inside: how a nuclear reactor turns uranium fission into steam and electricity, why the chain reaction is controllable, what the pressurised and boiling water designs actually do, the fuel cycle from ore to fuel assembly, radioactive waste and where it goes, radiation dose in numbers you can compare, what Three Mile Island, Chernobyl and Fukushima each taught, and why the money — not the physics — is the hard part.

sections.heading: A reactor is a kettle with an unusual firebox
sections.body: Strip away the containment dome and the security fence and a nuclear power station is a steam plant. Heat boils water, steam spins a turbine, the turbine spins a generator, and the generator pushes current onto the grid. The turbine hall of a nuclear station would be recognisable to an engineer from a coal plant of the same vintage, because it is essentially the same machine. Everything distinctive about nuclear power is upstream of the steam, in how the heat is made. In a coal or gas plant, heat comes from a chemical reaction: carbon and hydrogen combining with oxygen, rearranging the outer electrons of atoms. In a reactor it comes from splitting the nucleus itself, and the difference in scale is the whole point. Burning one carbon atom releases about 4 electronvolts. Splitting one uranium-235 nucleus releases about 200 million electronvolts — roughly fifty million times more energy from one event. That ratio is why the fuel is measured in tonnes rather than trainloads. A single gram of uranium-235, fully fissioned, yields about a megawatt-day of heat, which is around 23,000 kilowatt-hours, the energy in something like three and a half tonnes of coal. A fuel assembly you could lift with a crane runs a city block for years. The consequence that shapes everything else is that the fuel is small and the waste is small, and because both are small they are concentrated. A coal plant's waste is dispersed up a chimney by the million tonnes and into ash ponds by the hundred thousand; nobody guards it, and its harm is diffuse and statistical. A reactor's waste fits in a room, and it is intensely radioactive. Nuclear power trades a diffuse, unavoidable, continuous harm for a concentrated, containable, occasionally catastrophic one. Almost every argument about the technology is really an argument about whether that is a good trade, and reasonable people weigh concentrated and diffuse risk differently. The second consequence is inertia. Chemical combustion stops when you stop feeding it fuel or air. A reactor's chain reaction stops in about a second when you drop the control rods, but the fuel does not go cold, because the fragments left behind by fission are themselves radioactive and keep decaying whether you want them to or not. That residual heat is the reason a reactor needs cooling long after it has been shut down, and it is the direct cause of the two worst civil accidents in the technology's history. A fire you can put out; a reactor you have to keep cooling. Everything that follows in this guide is an elaboration of those three facts. The energy density is enormous, which makes the fuel cheap and the plant expensive. The material is concentrated, which makes containment both possible and essential. And the heat does not switch off, which is why the engineering is dominated not by making power but by removing heat reliably under every condition anyone has thought of, including the loss of the grid connection the plant is there to serve.

sections.heading: The chain reaction, and the accident of physics that makes it controllable
sections.body: A uranium-235 nucleus that absorbs a neutron becomes briefly uranium-236, wobbles, and splits into two lighter nuclei — typically something around krypton and something around barium, though the split is not fixed. It also throws out two or three free neutrons. If, on average, exactly one of those neutrons goes on to cause another fission, the reaction sustains itself at a steady rate. That average is called k, the multiplication factor. At k = 1 the reactor is critical, which in the trade simply means running steadily; it is not a warning word. Below 1 the reaction dies away, above 1 it grows. Natural uranium will not do this on its own in an ordinary reactor. It is 99.3 per cent uranium-238, which absorbs neutrons without usefully fissioning, and only 0.7 per cent uranium-235, which is the isotope that splits. Most reactors therefore run on fuel enriched to between three and five per cent uranium-235. This is worth stating plainly because it is the source of a persistent public confusion: a weapon needs uranium enriched to something like ninety per cent, more than an order of magnitude further along a difficult and conspicuous industrial process. A power reactor's fuel cannot explode like a bomb, and not because of any safety system — the physics simply is not there. Whatever else goes wrong at a nuclear plant, and things do, a nuclear explosion is not on the list. The part that makes control possible at all is a quirk. If every neutron from fission appeared instantly, a reactor would be ungovernable. The average time between one fission and the next it causes is about a ten-thousandth of a second, so a reactor even slightly above critical would double its power faster than any mechanical system could respond, and far faster than any human. But roughly 0.65 per cent of the neutrons from uranium-235 fission are not prompt. They come out of certain unstable fission fragments seconds to minutes after the split that made them. These are the delayed neutrons, and although they are a tiny minority they dominate the timing, because a reactor is operated in the narrow band where it is subcritical on prompt neutrons alone and relies on the delayed ones to close the gap to k = 1. In that band the reactor's response time is set not by ten-thousandths of a second but by the half-lives of those fragments — tens of seconds. Power changes then happen at a pace an operator can watch on a dial and a control system can comfortably manage. Reactor operators call the boundary of that band prompt criticality, and staying below it is the single most important rule in the trade. Chernobyl crossed it. The safety of every civil reactor running today rests, at bottom, on a 0.65 per cent accident of nuclear physics that nobody designed and that happens to be exactly what makes the technology usable.

sections.heading: Moderation: why the neutrons have to be slowed down
sections.body: Neutrons come out of fission fast — around fourteen thousand kilometres per second, carrying a couple of million electronvolts. At that speed they are surprisingly poor at causing further fission. Uranium-235 is far more likely to capture a slow neutron than a fast one; the difference is a factor of hundreds. So a reactor that runs on low-enriched uranium has to slow its neutrons down before they escape or are absorbed uselessly. The material that does this is the moderator, and the choice of moderator is the single biggest fork in reactor design. Slowing a neutron means making it bounce off something. Momentum does the rest: a neutron that hits a heavy nucleus rebounds like a marble off a bowling ball, losing almost nothing, while one that hits a nucleus of about its own mass can lose most of its energy in a single collision. The ideal moderator is therefore made of light nuclei. Hydrogen is the lightest of all, which is why ordinary water is the commonest moderator on earth, and why the phrase "light water reactor" covers the great majority of the world's fleet. Ordinary water has one drawback: hydrogen does not only scatter neutrons, it sometimes absorbs one and becomes deuterium. That loss is why light water reactors need enriched fuel — enrichment buys back the neutrons the moderator eats. Heavy water, in which the hydrogen is already deuterium, has almost no appetite for further neutrons, so a heavy water reactor can run on unenriched natural uranium. Canada's CANDU design does exactly this, which is attractive if you would rather not build an enrichment plant, and comes at the cost of producing heavy water, which is itself expensive. Graphite is the third classic choice: carbon is heavier than hydrogen so it takes more collisions, but it absorbs almost nothing, and it is a solid that tolerates high temperatures. Britain's gas-cooled reactors and the Soviet RBMK both used it. The moderator choice cascades into everything. It sets the enrichment you need, which sets the fuel supply chain. It sets whether the coolant and moderator are the same substance, which sets what happens when you lose the coolant. And that last point is where the deepest safety property of the common designs lives. In a light water reactor, water is both moderator and coolant. Lose the water, or let it boil into steam, and you lose the moderation — the neutrons stay fast, fission falls off, and the chain reaction shuts itself down. The reactor's response to losing its coolant is to stop reacting. This is called a negative void coefficient, and it is not a system that can fail; it is a property of the physics, active whether or not anyone is awake. A graphite-moderated, water-cooled design does not have it, because losing the water removes a neutron absorber while leaving the moderator in place. The RBMK at Chernobyl was of that kind, and at low power its void coefficient was positive: boiling made it more reactive, not less. That is the difference between a design whose physics argues with an accident and one whose physics joins in.

sections.heading: Control: rods, boron, and the feedback that acts faster than any operator
sections.body: Control rods are the part everyone can picture: neutron-hungry metal on a shaft, driven into the core to soak up neutrons and stop the reaction, withdrawn to let it run. The materials are chosen for appetite — boron, usually as boron carbide, and cadmium, hafnium and silver-indium-cadmium alloys. Dropping them all in is called a scram or a trip, and it takes a couple of seconds. In most designs gravity does it, and the electromagnets that hold the rods up release when power is lost, so a station blackout drops the rods rather than stranding them. Failing towards shutdown is a principle, not a coincidence. Rods are the coarse instrument. Pressurised water reactors also carry boron dissolved in the coolant itself — chemical shim — whose concentration is trimmed slowly over weeks to track the fuel's gradual burn-up. That leaves the rods free for fine adjustment and emergency use rather than being constantly worked. Boiling water reactors, which cannot use soluble boron in normal operation because the boiling would concentrate it unevenly, instead vary the flow of coolant through the core: push more water through and you get less steam, more moderation and more power. It is control by pump rather than by chemistry. But the control that matters most is not operated by anyone. Two feedback effects act on the fuel directly, in milliseconds, without instruction. The first is the Doppler effect in uranium-238. As fuel heats up, the nuclei in it jiggle faster, which smears out the energies at which uranium-238 absorbs neutrons and widens its capture bands. A hotter core therefore eats more of its own neutrons. Power rises, temperature rises, absorption rises, power falls. It is a thermostat built into the fuel pellets, it responds as fast as the fuel heats, and there is nothing to fail. The second is the void and temperature coefficient of the moderator described earlier: in a light water reactor, hotter and less dense water moderates less well, so power falls. Between them these two effects mean a properly designed light water core resists its own excursions. An operator error that would send an unstable design running away is instead met, within a fraction of a second, by physics pushing back. This is why the language of "safety systems" undersells modern reactor safety and, oddly, undermines confidence in it. Systems can fail, and people rightly discount them. The Doppler coefficient is not a system. Designers speak of defence in depth — the fuel's own feedback, then the cladding, then the pressure vessel, then the containment building, then the emergency cooling, then the site's exclusion zone — and the innermost layer, the one that acts first and never needs power, is not built at all. It is chosen, at the design stage, by picking a core whose physics is on your side.

sections.heading: The pressurised water reactor, and why most of the world runs one
sections.body: Around two-thirds of the world's power reactors are pressurised water reactors, and the design's dominance is more historical accident than considered choice: it descends from the compact reactor Admiral Rickover's programme developed for American submarines in the early 1950s, which needed to be small, tolerate a boat that pitches and rolls, and never boil in a hull full of sailors. Scaled up and put ashore, it became the industry's default. The trick in the name is that the water is kept under enough pressure not to boil. The primary circuit runs at about 155 bar — roughly 150 times atmospheric pressure — which raises water's boiling point past 340 °C. Coolant enters the core near 290 °C and leaves near 325 °C, hot enough to be useful, still liquid throughout. Keeping it liquid matters: liquid water carries heat far better than steam, and a core that never boils has no boiling to go wrong. That hot water does not go anywhere near the turbine. It flows to a steam generator, a vessel full of thousands of thin U-shaped tubes, and gives its heat through the tube walls to a completely separate secondary circuit at lower pressure, which does boil. The secondary steam drives the turbine, condenses, and returns. The two circuits touch only through metal. The point of that separation is that anything radioactive stays in the primary loop, inside containment, so the turbine hall is an ordinary industrial space that people walk through in overalls. It also means a leak in a steam generator tube is a serious event, because it is the one place where the two circuits are close enough to fail into each other. A pressuriser — a tall vessel part full of steam, with heaters and a cold-water spray — sits on the primary loop and holds the pressure steady, absorbing the expansion and contraction of the coolant as power changes. It is the shock absorber of the system, and its relief valve was the component that stuck open at Three Mile Island. The reactor vessel itself is a steel forging with walls of the order of twenty centimetres thick, holding a core of a couple of hundred fuel assemblies, each a bundle of a few hundred slender zirconium-alloy tubes packed with uranium dioxide pellets. Around all of it stands the containment: a steel-lined, prestressed concrete structure typically about a metre thick, designed to hold the pressure of the entire primary circuit flashing to steam, and incidentally to survive an aircraft impact. The design's virtues are its separation of circuits, its strongly negative feedback, and half a century of accumulated operating experience across hundreds of units. Its vices are that everything runs at very high pressure, which makes the vessel and piping enormous and expensive engineering; and that thermal efficiency is only around 33 to 35 per cent, well below a modern gas plant, because the steam is limited to what pressurised water can deliver. Two-thirds of the heat goes into a river, the sea, or a cooling tower.

sections.heading: Boiling water, heavy water, gas and the designs that took another road
sections.body: The boiling water reactor is the pressurised design's obvious simplification: if the steam has to be made anyway, why not make it in the core? A BWR runs at about 75 bar, lets the water boil among the fuel, and pipes the steam straight to the turbine. Out go the steam generators, the pressuriser and the second circuit; the pressure vessel is larger but the plant is simpler and thermally much the same. The price is that the turbine now handles slightly radioactive steam, mostly from nitrogen-16 produced in the coolant, so the turbine hall is a controlled area during operation. Nitrogen-16 has a seven-second half-life, so the hall is safe to enter shortly after shutdown, but you cannot wander in mid-shift. BWRs also control power partly by coolant flow, which gives them a smooth response to load changes. CANDU, the Canadian deuterium-uranium design, takes the heavy water road. Because heavy water barely absorbs neutrons, it runs on natural uranium, sidestepping enrichment entirely. Instead of one big pressure vessel it uses hundreds of horizontal pressure tubes running through a tank of cool heavy water moderator, and that geometry allows refuelling while the reactor is at full power, pushing fresh bundles in one end and spent ones out the other. High availability is the reward. The drawbacks are the cost of heavy water, a positive void coefficient requiring careful design compensation, and the fact that on-load refuelling is exactly the capability that makes a reactor useful for producing weapons-grade plutonium, which has made the design politically sensitive to export. Britain went its own way twice. The Magnox reactors and their successors, the advanced gas-cooled reactors, use graphite as moderator and carbon dioxide as coolant, blowing gas at high pressure through channels in a graphite stack. Gas cooling allows much higher outlet temperatures — around 640 °C in an AGR — and therefore thermal efficiency above 40 per cent, the best of any commercial reactor type. The cost was engineering complexity, difficult construction and a fleet that was expensive to build and never exported. The Soviet RBMK combined graphite moderation with water cooling in pressure tubes, was cheap, could be built very large and refuelled on load, and had the positive void coefficient discussed earlier. The surviving units were substantially modified after 1986, and the type has been progressively retired. Fast reactors — sodium-cooled, unmoderated — are the road most often taken and least often finished. Without a moderator, fast neutrons can convert uranium-238 into plutonium faster than the plutonium is consumed, breeding more fuel than they burn and, in principle, extending uranium reserves by a factor of many tens. France, Russia, Japan, the United States and India have all built them; sodium, which burns in air and reacts violently with water, has made them difficult to operate reliably, and only Russia currently runs them commercially at scale. Small modular reactors are the current wave: factory-built units of tens to a few hundred megawatts, trucked to site, betting that serial production beats bespoke construction. The argument is economic rather than nuclear. Whether it is right is not yet settled by anything built and operating commercially in the West.

sections.heading: Decay heat: the problem that does not switch off
sections.body: Drop the control rods and fission stops within about a second. The reactor does not. The fission fragments accumulated in the fuel — iodine, caesium, strontium, xenon and a long tail of others — are unstable, and they go on decaying on their own schedules, releasing heat regardless of what the rods are doing. Immediately after shutdown this decay heat is about six to seven per cent of the reactor's full thermal power. For a large reactor producing three gigawatts of heat, that is around two hundred megawatts — the output of a decent-sized gas turbine, appearing inside a core that has just been shut down, with nobody able to turn it off. It falls away, but slowly and on a stubborn curve. After an hour it is around one per cent; after a day, a few tenths of a per cent; after a year, still enough that spent fuel must be actively cooled. Ten megawatts of unremovable heat in a sealed vessel is more than enough to boil the coolant away, uncover the fuel, and destroy it. This single fact is the organising problem of reactor safety, and understanding it explains why nuclear plants look the way they do. Multiple independent cooling trains, each able to do the job alone. Emergency core cooling that injects water under pressure. Diesel generators, usually several, to run the pumps when the grid is gone — and the grid is very often gone, because whatever knocked the plant offline may well have knocked the transmission out too. Batteries to bridge the minutes before the diesels start. Passive systems in newer designs that circulate coolant by natural convection and dump heat to a tank of water sitting above the reactor, needing no pump and no power at all, sometimes for three days unattended. Both of the accidents that destroyed reactor cores were decay-heat accidents. At Three Mile Island a relief valve stuck open, coolant escaped, and operators — misreading their instruments — throttled back the emergency injection that was doing exactly what it should. The chain reaction had stopped as designed; decay heat uncovered and melted about half the core anyway. At Fukushima Daiichi the reactors scrammed correctly on the earthquake, and then the tsunami flooded the emergency diesel generators, which were sited low. The plant lost the grid, then lost its backup power, and with it the ability to remove a heat load that would not stop. Cores melted over the following days. Neither accident involved a runaway chain reaction. Both were failures to remove heat from a reactor that was already shut down. That is the distinctive hazard of the technology, and it is why the correct question to ask of any reactor design is not "how does it stop?" — they all stop — but "how does it stay cool with no power, no operators and no water supply, and for how long?"

sections.heading: The fuel cycle: from ore in the ground to a bundle in the core
sections.body: Uranium is not rare. It is about as abundant in the earth's crust as tin, more common than silver by a wide margin, and present in seawater at three parts per billion. What is rare is uranium concentrated enough to be worth digging. Typical ore runs around a tenth of a per cent uranium; the exceptional deposits of Canada's Athabasca Basin run to fifteen or twenty per cent, which is why Canada, Kazakhstan, Namibia and Australia dominate supply. Increasingly the ore is not dug at all but dissolved in place by in-situ leaching, pumping a mild solution down one borehole and drawing uranium-bearing liquid up another. The mill produces yellowcake, a coarse uranium oxide powder, which is the form uranium is traded in. From there the sequence is fixed. Conversion turns the oxide into uranium hexafluoride, chosen because it becomes a gas at a convenient temperature and is therefore separable by isotope. Enrichment then raises the uranium-235 fraction from nature's 0.7 per cent to the three to five per cent a light water reactor needs. Modern enrichment is done by gas centrifuge: thousands of tubes spinning at enormous speed, each achieving a tiny separation, cascaded so the small effects compound. The older gaseous-diffusion plants that did this work through the twentieth century were vast and consumed something like a fiftieth of a nation's electricity; centrifuges do the same job for a fraction of the power, which is precisely why the technology is watched so closely. The industrial capability that makes reactor fuel is the same capability that, run for longer, makes weapons material. Everything about the international safeguards regime follows from this one fact. Fabrication presses the enriched material into ceramic uranium dioxide pellets about a centimetre across, sinters them at high temperature until they are hard and dense, grinds them to tolerance and stacks them in thin tubes of zirconium alloy. Zirconium is used because it is almost transparent to neutrons and stands up to hot water; its one bad habit, oxidising in high-temperature steam and liberating hydrogen, is the reason Fukushima's reactor buildings exploded. Sealed tubes are bundled into assemblies, and the assemblies are the units handled at the plant. Fuel stays in the core for four to six years, typically with a third of the assemblies replaced every eighteen months or two years. It is not consumed evenly, and it is not consumed much: modern burn-up is around forty-five to fifty gigawatt-days per tonne, which sounds impressive and means only a few per cent of the original uranium's energy has been extracted. What limits it is not the fuel running out but the cladding, the accumulation of neutron-absorbing fission products, and the mechanical state of the assembly. What comes out is called spent fuel, and the name is a considerable overstatement — most of the energy is still in it, which is the argument for reprocessing and the whole reason fast reactors are of interest.

sections.heading: What comes out: spent fuel, and the honest state of the waste question
sections.body: A spent fuel assembly is roughly ninety-five per cent uranium-238, about one per cent uranium-235 still unburnt, about one per cent plutonium bred from the uranium-238, and three or four per cent fission products and minor actinides. It is thermally hot and intensely radioactive — unshielded, it would deliver a lethal dose in minutes — and both properties decline steeply. Fresh from the core it goes into a storage pool, water being an excellent shield and coolant, for at least five years and often much longer. After that it can move to dry cask storage: sealed steel canisters inside concrete overpacks, standing on a pad in the open, cooled by nothing but the air moving past them. Two things about the quantity are worth stating clearly, because the public argument tends to lose both. The volume is small. All the spent fuel ever produced by the entire United States civil programme, over some seven decades, would cover a single football pitch to a depth of about ten metres. And it is not going anywhere on its own: it is a solid ceramic in a sealed metal tube in a concrete cask, not a liquid, not a gas, and not something that leaks quietly into a river. The disposal problem is genuinely hard, but it is hard in the way that a bank vault is hard, not in the way that carbon dioxide is hard. The timescale is the sting. The fission products — the caesium and strontium that make spent fuel dangerous now — have half-lives of about thirty years and are down to background levels within roughly three hundred. It is the minor actinides, plutonium and americium and neptunium, that produce the hundred-thousand-year figures. Reprocessing, which chemically separates the uranium and plutonium for reuse, both recovers usable fuel and sharply reduces the volume and longevity of what remains. France does it at La Hague and burns the product as mixed-oxide fuel; the United States stopped in the 1970s on the deliberate policy judgment that separated plutonium is a proliferation risk not worth taking, and has not restarted. The long-term answer everyone agrees on in principle is deep geological disposal: several hundred metres down, in a stable rock formation that has demonstrably not moved or admitted water for millions of years. The engineering is not the obstacle. Finland has built one, at Onkalo in bedrock that has been quiet since long before there were humans to worry about it; Sweden has approved a similar site. Almost everywhere else the obstacle has been political, most famously at Yucca Mountain in Nevada, which absorbed decades and billions of dollars of study before being defunded in 2010 over the objections of a state that did not want it. The honest summary is that the waste problem is solved technically and unsolved politically, and that the interim answer — casks on a pad under guard — works, is monitored, and was never meant to be permanent.

sections.heading: Three accidents, and what each one actually taught
sections.body: Three civil accidents dominate the technology's reputation, and they taught genuinely different lessons. Conflating them, in either direction, is the commonest error in the argument. Three Mile Island, Pennsylvania, 1979. A relief valve on the pressuriser stuck open and the control room had no direct indication of it — the instrument showed the signal sent to the valve, not the valve's actual position. Coolant escaped for hours. Misreading a rising water level in the pressuriser as a full system, operators cut back the emergency injection that was keeping the core covered. About half the core melted. The containment held, and offsite radiation exposure was of the order of a chest X-ray at most; no deaths or detectable health effects have been attributed to it. The lesson was about human factors, not physics. Control rooms were redesigned, instrumentation was changed to show what things are doing rather than what they were told to do, simulator training became mandatory, and an industry body was created to police operational standards. It was, in engineering terms, a containment success and a control-room failure. Chernobyl, Ukraine, 1986. A badly conceived low-power test, run by a crew who had disabled safety systems to complete it, drove an RBMK reactor into exactly the region where its positive void coefficient made it unstable. Power ran away in seconds through prompt criticality; the reactor destroyed itself in a steam explosion, the graphite burned, and there was no Western-style containment building to hold any of it. This was a real catastrophe: two workers died immediately, twenty-eight more of acute radiation syndrome within months, and around six thousand thyroid cancers followed among people who were children at the time and drank contaminated milk — a toll that mass distribution of iodine tablets and a milk ban would have largely prevented. The lesson was about design and institutions: do not build a reactor with a positive void coefficient, do build a containment, and do not run a safety culture in which a test schedule outranks a shutdown limit. Fukushima Daiichi, Japan, 2011. A magnitude 9.0 earthquake; the reactors scrammed correctly. Then a tsunami far above the design basis flooded the emergency diesel generators, which had been sited low. With the grid down and the diesels drowned, there was no way to remove decay heat. Three cores melted over the following days and hydrogen from the zirconium-steam reaction blew the tops off the reactor buildings. The radiological toll was strikingly small — no deaths attributable to radiation, and one worker's later cancer officially compensated. But the evacuation itself killed on the order of two thousand people, mostly elderly, through the disruption of care and the stress of displacement. That is the most uncomfortable finding in the whole field: at Fukushima, the response to the radiation did far more harm than the radiation, and this is now taken seriously in emergency planning rather than dismissed.

sections.heading: Radiation dose, in numbers you can actually compare
sections.body: Almost every public argument about nuclear power founders on the absence of a scale. Radiation is reported in units nobody uses for anything else and in quantities separated by factors of a million, so "radiation detected" and "radiation dangerous" become the same headline. The unit worth learning is the sievert, which measures biological dose, and the practical unit is the millisievert, a thousandth of one, or the microsievert, a millionth. Eating a banana is about 0.1 microsieverts, from its natural potassium-40. A dental X-ray is roughly 5. A transatlantic flight is 30 to 50, because at altitude there is less atmosphere overhead to stop cosmic rays. A chest X-ray is around 100 microsieverts, which is 0.1 millisieverts. An abdominal CT scan is about 8 millisieverts — that is, some eighty chest X-rays, which is worth knowing before consenting to one casually. The number to anchor everything else against is natural background: about 2.4 millisieverts a year on average worldwide, from cosmic rays, from radon seeping out of the ground, from potassium in your own body, and from the rocks around you. It varies enormously by geology. Parts of Cornwall, Kerala and Ramsar in Iran run several times the average, and in the highest natural-background places on earth residents receive tens of millisieverts a year with no detected excess of disease. Occupational limits for radiation workers are set at 20 millisieverts a year averaged over five years. The level at which epidemiology can actually detect an increase in cancer risk is around 100 millisieverts of accumulated dose; below that, the increase, if there is one, is too small to separate from the ordinary variation in cancer rates. Acute radiation sickness begins around 1000 millisieverts — one sievert — delivered at once, and around five sieverts acute is lethal to roughly half of people without intensive treatment. The gap between those figures is the crux. A dose that a monitor can measure easily and report alarmingly may be a thousandth of the level at which any effect has ever been observed. Below 100 millisieverts, safety regulation uses the linear no-threshold model, which assumes risk continues proportionally all the way down to zero. It is a deliberately cautious administrative assumption rather than a measured fact, and it is a sensible one for setting worker limits. Used as a prediction — multiplying a minuscule dose by a large population to compute expected deaths — it produces numbers that sound authoritative and rest on an extrapolation the model's own authors do not endorse. If you take one thing from this section, take the habit of asking for a number and a comparison before forming a view.

sections.heading: What it costs, and why the money is the genuinely hard part
sections.body: Nuclear power has an unusual cost structure and nearly all of its difficulties are downstream of it. The fuel is almost free — uranium is a few per cent of the cost of the electricity, so a fuel price shock that would wreck a gas plant barely registers. Operating costs are moderate and predictable. Capital costs are enormous, and they arrive years before a single unit of electricity is sold. For a modern Western reactor, something like sixty to eighty per cent of the lifetime cost of the electricity is the cost of building the plant and the interest on the money borrowed to do it. This makes the schedule, not the engineering, the decisive variable. A project financed at seven per cent that runs five years late has accumulated an enormous interest bill on capital that is earning nothing, and this is why nuclear projects do not fail slowly and expensively — they fail by being late, and the lateness is what makes them expensive. The recent Western record is poor and there is no use dressing it up. Flamanville 3 in France was begun in 2007 with a budget in the low billions of euros and connected to the grid in 2024 at several times that. Hinkley Point C in Britain has seen its estimate rise repeatedly across its construction. Vogtle units 3 and 4 in Georgia came in around seven years late and at roughly double the original figure, and bankrupted their reactor vendor along the way. The common thread is first-of-a-kind construction by workforces and supply chains that had not built a reactor in decades, to designs still being finalised as concrete was poured. The counter-examples matter as much. South Korea built a fleet of standardised units on schedule and at a fraction of Western cost, and exported that capability to build four reactors at Barakah in the United Arab Emirates broadly to plan. China builds reliably and quickly. What distinguishes them is not different physics or laxer regulation but repetition: the same design, the same firms, the same crews, one project after another, so the learning curve is climbed rather than restarted. Nuclear construction rewards a programme and punishes a one-off, which is exactly what most Western countries have attempted for forty years. Two further costs are real and often argued about dishonestly in both directions. Decommissioning a reactor costs a substantial sum and takes decades, and in most countries operators are legally required to accumulate a fund for it during operation rather than presenting the bill later. Long-term waste management is similarly levied on the electricity sold. These are internalised in a way that the atmospheric disposal of combustion products is not, which is the fairest single sentence anyone can offer about how the technology's costs compare with its alternatives.

sections.heading: Where nuclear fits alongside wind and solar
sections.body: Nuclear supplies roughly a tenth of the world's electricity and about a quarter of its low-carbon electricity. The share is concentrated: France draws around two-thirds of its power from reactors, and a handful of countries account for most of the rest. Measured over the full lifecycle — mining, enrichment, construction, operation, decommissioning — the IPCC's assessed median is about twelve grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per kilowatt-hour, which puts it alongside wind and below solar, and one to two orders of magnitude below coal or gas. On the grounds of carbon it is not a marginal case. Its operational character is baseload: high capital cost, near-zero marginal cost, and a strong economic incentive to run flat out. Modern plants achieve capacity factors above ninety per cent, producing at night, in still air, in winter, and through the weather events that matter most to a grid. That is the property nothing else on a low-carbon system supplies at scale without either storage or fuel. The awkwardness is that this profile fits badly with the one that variable renewables produce. A grid with a large solar fleet has hours of near-zero or negative wholesale prices in the middle of sunny days, and a plant whose costs are almost entirely fixed loses money in every one of them. The French fleet does load-follow, adjusting output substantially over a day, so the claim that reactors technically cannot is false. The claim that it is economic for them to is much weaker: throttling back a plant whose fuel is nearly free saves almost nothing and forgoes revenue that was supposed to pay off the construction loan. The honest framing is that nuclear and variable renewables are neither straightforward substitutes nor natural partners. They compete for the same low-carbon investment, and on a grid that has already built out a lot of one, the value of the other changes. What both are competing against, in practice, is gas, whose flexibility is currently what keeps the lights on when the wind drops. Nuclear's remaining advantages are density and reliability. A reactor site occupies a very small footprint for the energy it delivers, which matters where land is contested. It is indifferent to weather. Its fuel can be stockpiled for years in a warehouse, which is a strategic consideration that several countries have re-learned recently. Its disadvantages are that it is slow to build, expensive to finance, dependent on a construction capability most Western countries let wither, and politically fragile in a way that no other generating technology is — a single accident anywhere in the world changes policy everywhere. Whether it deserves a large role is a question about cost, speed and public consent. It has not, for some decades, been a question about whether the physics works.
